speakerposition: topic
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, December 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Garson for the second reading of Bill No. 36, to amend the Combines Investigation Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate, but because there have been so many speeches-many of them more or less to the point-from the official opposition side of the house, I felt I should give some reasons why, as a member of the government, I was of the opinion that this legislation should be supported. For that reason I should like to speak briefly on the subject of the legislation which the government has proposed to deal with resale price maintenance.
Any delay in the consideration of this legislation, as the Prime Minister has said, is not in the government's view in the interests of the public at large. Either we are serious about this matter or we are not. Nor do I think that the alternative measures which have been proposed are likely to produce the results that the people of Canada want. Let me give you some reasons for believing that we should reject the tactics, the delaying tactics, which have been submitted as alternative proposals to this house by those who have moved various amendments, and those who have supported those amendments with speeches.
After the prolonged consideration that has been given to the proposed legislation on resale price maintenance, there is perhaps little for me to say. When I hear, however, members from the opposition side of the house suggest that this matter is being rushed through without due consideration to a conclusion, I wonder what more could reasonably be asked from this side of the house.
Hon. members will recall first of all that the royal commission on prices under the chairmanship of Professor Clifford Curtis of Queen's university was-and I quote his remarks-"impressed by the degree to which individual manufacturers fix the sale prices of their products, and so narrow the area in which price competition amongst wholesalers and retailers is operative."
2442	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act
That commission, which included a representative of the women of Canada, in the person of Mrs. Sutherland, and a prominent representative of the Quebec co-operative movement, Mr. Bois, recommended that the combines investigation commission give careful consideration and study to the problem, with a view to devising measures to deal with it.
Then, later on, we had the MacQuarrie committee, an impartial and distinguished group of Canadians who made a study of resale price maintenance and reached the unanimous recommendation that the practice is not in the public interest and should be made illegal. That was a unanimous recommendation, and there was no reservation to it whatever.
There has been criticism of that report on the ground that the committee did not obtain sufficient factual evidence. I am not much impressed by that kind of criticism. What I think is significant is that men like Mr. Justice MacQuarrie from Nova Scotia, and Mr. Curtis from British Columbia, Mr. Lamontagne from Quebec and Dr. Mackintosh from Queen's university, Kingston, Ontario, were satisfied that they had enough information to reach the unanimous conclusion that resale price maintenance is not in the public interest. I am quite sure that if they had felt that more information was required before reaching such a conclusion they would not have hesitated to say so.
Nevertheless a joint committee of parliament was established. That committee sat for days. It heard representations from leading organizations who did not agree with the findings of the MacQuarrie committee. Of course, the committee could have sat for a much longer period of time. After reading the evidence presented to the committee I am satisfied, and I think the great majority of members of the house are satisfied, that the MacQuarrie committee's conclusions were well founded and that there is every reason to take immediate action.
In addition to the study given to resale price maintenance by the royal commission on prices, by the MacQuarrie committee and the joint parliamentary committee, we have been discussing this matter in the house for many, many days.
But what is the position of the official opposition in the matter? The truth is that they have no policy. They would like to get credit from those who benefit from resale price maintenance for preventing the passage of the legislation. On the other hand, they attempt to justify their position to the consumers and the general public by asking for more consideration.


Yet the fact of the matter is that the official opposition have spent a good deal of the time during which they might have debated the merits of the legislation talking about not having enough time.
Yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) refuted the suggestion that the government is not wholeheartedly behind this legislation. I wish to associate myself most strongly with the words of the Prime Minister, as I am sure every member on this side of the house would want to do. It is my view that the legislation is in the public interest, in the interests of consumers; and because it is in the interests of consumers, it is also in the interest of manufacturers and the distributive trades as well.
An attempt has been made to create the impression that this legislation is detrimental to the business life of Canada. I see no reason to think that that will be the ease. The legislation should result in increased competition among distributors. At least it will remove one of the barriers to competition. Is that a good thing? I believe that it is. I do not believe any efficient business need fear competition. I know that many businessmen, large and small, share this view and admire the government's courage in introducing this legislation.
It would have been possible, of course, for the government to shut its eyes to the problems created by the growing practice of resale price maintenance. We could have let well enough alone. But, as I see it, it is the duty of the government to be vigilant where the public interest is concerned. Resale price maintenance may be relatively harmless in some cases; but in other cases, as the Curtis commission, the MacQuarrie committee and the joint parliamentary committee have pointed out, it is a grave and growing abuse.
It is a fact that business prospers when it is free to serve the public to the best of its ability, with as few restrictions as possible, whether imposed by governments or by private arrangements.
On the whole, we know that Canadian business is efficient, and I would like to see it become more efficient, more able to supply Canadian consumers with goods of the highest quality at the lowest possible prices. The evidence we have before us from these various commissions and committees, and the facts that have come to my personal attention, lead me to believe that the practice of resale price maintenance does not lead to consumers obtaining full advantage of competition. That is why I support this legislation.

In my judgment it is not going to lead to any revolutionary change in business practices or in prices. But what change there is will be in the right direction. When prices could or should be reduced, those reductions will come about more readily and more quickly. There will be more flexibility in the system.
We shall, I believe, be better able to meet competition from imported goods. As hon. members are probably aware, there is already a good deal of competition for the Canadian consumer's dollar from producers in other countries. It is logical to believe that there will be more competition if, as we hope, the world recovers from its present difficulties and the imminent threat of war is removed. For that reason alone I think we should support all measures that help to make Canadian business more efficient and better able to hold its own. We cannot afford to become flabby and to rely upon restrictive practices to support the inefficient.
Merchants who find themselves with stocks of goods which are moving too slowly will be able to reduce their prices in order to overcome consumer resistance, without endangering their future sources of supply. Consumers will be able to shop about, to get greater advantage from being able to pay cash, or from finding some merchant who, because of location or volume or for some other reason, is able to offer goods at a lower price.
As several members have pointed out, the effect on the cost of living will probably not be very substantial. It may be that the effect upon the cost of living index itself will be quite modest, partly because the index does not fully reflect reductions below regular prices, but that is not a reason for not going ahead with the legislation. There are many anti-inflationary measures which do not individually and by themselves affect the cost of living very much, but they are worth doing, nevertheless, as part of a general policy of restraining price rises and bringing about price reductions.
Already there have been four amendments to this legislation moved by members of the official opposition. There has been more time consumed with reference to this legislation than has been consumed in connection with a number of other matters which the house thought and which members of the official opposition thought should have taken more time than in fact they did. What I am trying to say is that practically every alternative has been canvassed with reference to this legislation and I feel that the time has arrived -I think the house is of the same opinion-
Combines Investigation Act when we should no longer delay its passage. Therefore I move, seconded by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin):
That the question be now put.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. It must be embarrassing at this particular stage when I think the house expected the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) to have his opportunity to conclude the debate by replying, to find another member of the government entering the debate and reading a prepared statement. I think it must have been pretty embarrassing to the Minister of Justice to sit there and, at the point where normally as mover of the motion that this bill be read a second time he would reply, to have to sit back and listen to one of his colleagues make a speech setting out the government line. The statement just read by the Minister of Transport simply followed the government line.
What purpose that statement was intended to serve apparently will be left to the house to guess, but the motion which has been put before the house at least exposes to naked view what has been attempted here by the government in various ways for some days past, that is, to throttle discussion on this bill and to prevent adequate consideration of the important subject involved in the measure.
The motion that the question be now put is designed to stop the discussion of the measure on second reading. This being the government's position, this being the determination of the government, I hope that hon. members who are now called to step into line and vote as the government demands wiJi
2444	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act have in mind that they are in this way giving endorsement to government action to stop further discussion of one of the most important measures which have confronted the Canadian parliament.
The fact that this measure has already run the course of debate for some time, the fact that it has given rise to a good deal of discussion in the house and outside, the fact that it is a measure which demands and deserves the study of the house will create a lasting indictment of this attempt on the part of the government, or this further stage in the attempt that the government has made in recent days, to throttle discussion of the bill.
The Minister of Transport said something this morning about getting along with this measure, that there had been enough discussion already in the house. If we do not hear anything more from the government than we have heard thus far one question will remain unanswered to the end of time as far as this debate is concerned. That question is this: Why was it necessary that such haste be displayed in this whole undertaking, that the parliamentary committee should not have been permitted to conduct a proper, adequate and thorough investigation? Why was it so urgent that it should have been left to a Liberal majority in that parliamentary committee to deny a hearing to people whose businesses stand in jeopardy in the light of this measure? Why was it so urgent that people should be told, people who had serious interests at stake and serious views to lay before the parliamentary committee, that the committee had no time to hear them? Why was it that organizations representing thousands of retailers in this country were denied access to and hearing by that committee?
Those questions remain unanswered. The government says that it is necessary that the house proceed with haste. I want to say to the Minister of Transport, whose acquaintance with this subject may have been a little recent, that he has a great big question to answer, a question which remained unanswered in his speech this morning.
Here is a practice which has been established in many lines of retail merchandising. It is a practice that has existed in some lines of merchandise since early in the century, and in many other important lines for at least twenty-five years. That practice has existed for that length of time within the knowledge of this government which has been in office since 1935, and yet in all those years this government, with that practice existing right under its nose, did not make the slightest move to stop or interfere with


it. But suddenly in the fall of 1951, like a bolt from the blue, without the slightest warning, it becomes a matter of life-and-death urgency. Why?
Let the Minister of Transport tell us why this practice has gone on under the nose of this government since the government came into office in October, 1935, for more than sixteen years, without their moving a finger to interfere with it. Let him tell us why in the fall of 1951 it has become a matter of life-and-death urgency, a matter which will brook no delay, a matter which could not even wait until there had been an adequate study and understanding of the matter in a parliamentary committee appointed for the purpose and then throttled by government decision?
We have been told that the father of the Combines Investigation Act was the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King. Mr. McGregor was the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act all the way through the late Mr. King's tenure of office as prime minister-yes, up until the fall of 1949 when he resigned rather than submit to further indignities at the hands of this government and to being a knowing party to a continued breach of the law of this country by the government.
Since this legislation is piotured to us as a matter of life-and-death urgency, I tell the government and every Liberal member in this house who is being whipped into line to vote for second reading of this measure today that by their action they are condemning the govemiment of the late Mr. Mackenzie King. They are condemning what Mr. McGregor has done or failed to do during his long period of service as commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act. That is precisely what they are doing today. The government is proposing a vote of condemnation and censure upon the inaction of the late Mr. Mackenzie King and upon Mr. McGregor's stewardship in office over these long years because nothing was done then, and now whereas we of the official opposition say that this measure should have adequate study, the government's headlong rush now constitutes a blanket condemnation of all that has gone before it. I hope government supporters will weigh that fact well. I hope they will not overlook the fact that today, if they fall into line at the cracking of the government whip, they are giving a vote of condemnation on the government for what it has left undone in the past.
I will tell you why the government was so desperately anxious to make a show of doing something this fall. It was because the cost of living has soared out of sight, and

when the government was not prepared to abandon its outrageous taxation policies, which have been responsible for boosting the cost of living out of sight, it was politically essential that they should drum up some kind of hoax to delude the people of Canada into thinking that something was really being done-and a hoax this measure is. That is the only name it deserves. It was conceived as an attempt to delude the people of Canada, but the cat has been let out of the bag. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) has added his contribution this morning to the confession which has already escaped the lips of one or two members of the government, and has indicated that this measure if adopted is not going to have any perceptible effect on the cost of living. That is an undeniable fact, and in itself is an exposure of this hoax that the government is attempting to perpetrate.
The second feature of the hoax is this, and of course it is an example of the technique of one Adolf Hitler, the well known technique that when you are taking a line of action that is designed to play into the hands of one particular group then you get up and deny it. You deny that it is going to have that effeot, denounce those who are of that group who are going to be affected, and say that your measure is going to help somebody else. That is what we see taking place in this debate on the part of the orators opposite. Here is a measure which has been shown beyond any doubt whatever to be one that is sought by the big interests in the merchandising field. The biggest of the departmental stores are asking for it. The chains are going to benefit by it. It is the big interests in the merchandising field who are seeking this measure, and it is the little fellows in the merchandising field whose interests are at stake, the life of whose businesses in thousands of cases is in jeopardy and who are pleading for an opportunity to be heard and for fair consideration of their position.
Their position is a very important one. The small retailer in Canada represents as fine a flowering of the system of free enterprise in this country as you will find. Yet the government is placing that small retailer in jeopardy by their insistence on jamming this measure through. This hoax again is exposed as a callous attempt on the part of the government, in league with big interests, to hurt the interests of the little retailer. That is the second feature of this monstrous government hoax. We have not heard from the Minister of Transport this morning one word of concern about the fate of the little retailers. There has not been a suggestion of concern for their plight in face of the threat of the
Combines Investigation Act loss leader practice. The minister cannot deny that branded goods, the kind that are subject to the practice of resale price maintenance in Canada today, are the goods that are by their very nature the kind that the big merchandisers like to seize upon for the purpose of loss leaders. After all, sir, what is the use of the retailer selecting for his loss leader some article that is not branded, that is not the subject of national advertising, -that has not a known price? The public could not then estimate the alleged reduction in price, but goods that are subject to resale price maintenance are those that naturally lend themselves to use as loss leaders by the big merchandising outlets. That, sir, is what is going to happen, and it does not matter to the government that those who know their own business best are pleading for consideration in face of the threat of the harm that will be done to their businesses by the loss leader practice.
The government has not the time to listen to them. The government is too busy pursuing through this measure its political purposes, its base partisan purposes, even to listen to those who are pleading for the existence of their businesses. Not a word fell from the lips of the minister this morning on the subject of loss leaders. Yesterday we heard the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) call for an election on this issue. I would remind the house that in the committee the hon. member for Spadina at least was concerned about the loss leader practice. He was at least concerned enough over the threat that the loss leader offers to the business of the small retailer that he-and I give him credit for it -drafted legislation to illegalize the loss leader practice. States by the state of California. They were not evidence, only statements of opinion. One would have thought that, if there were such evidence, the government would have been willing and anxious to bring it forward. The only conclusion to which one can come from their failure to do so, and from their obvious and successful desire to choke off discussion and to prevent us from getting such evidence, is that actually the evidence, if it were produced, would tend the other way.
There is, however, ample evidence to the effect that the small retailer will be hurt if the practice of resale price maintenance is eliminated. In the light of that evidence, we are left with the question, why is the government in such a hurry to hurt the small retailer? Why are they in such a hurry to remove the only protection which the small retailer has against the power of the big interests, the monopolies and the large chain stores, and leave him at the mercy of cutthroat competition? No satisfactory answer to that question has yet been given; yet the Prime Minister, in taking part in this debate yesterday, said that the government was not willing to leave this matter over for any further or fuller investigation; that they were going to remove the protection from the small retailer and leave him to stand on his own feet. It is a callous, ill-considered and ill-advised course to follow, with much harm to be done to independent Canadian business.
In dealing with this matter I believe it is important to remember that the evidence we have does not support, but indeed directly contradicts, the propaganda efforts which the government have been making to convince the Canadian people that it is the big interests that want this practice of resale price maintenance, and particularly the propaganda put forward by the government to the effect that it is the manufacturer who wants resale price maintenance. Nothing can be further from the


truth; nothing can be more directly in conflict with the evidence which we have. The evidence which we had in the committee on this point showed most clearly that it is not at the instance of the manufacturer that resale price maintenance prevails, but that the practice was worked out and applied by and at the request of the small retailers who found it essential as a measure to protect them from the unfair types of competition being indulged in by the big interests. Once again I refer particularly to the evidence of Mr. Fred McGregor, who answered that question perhaps more clearly and with less hesitation than he answered any other questions in his whole evidence-and his answers to questions were on the whole not given in a hesitant manner; but of all the questions which were asked he was perhaps most definite in his reply to the questions as to who wants this most, who benefits most from it, the manufacturer or the retailer? His answer was, "unquestionably the retailer".
It is also important to bear in mind that *there is nothing before this house, as there was nothing before the committee, on which we would be justified in basing the conclusion that the removal of resale price maintenance will benefit the consumer with respect to prices. Indeed, there is much before us to justify the conclusion that it will harm the consumer in the long run both generally and with respect to prices, and if for no other reason than that it will result in the further concentration of power and control over the distributive trades in the hands of a few huge concerns, a tendency from which we already suffer in Canada to a degree greater than in any comparable country. There can be no question but that the result of that process, in the long run, will be to damage the interests of the consumer. That has always been the outcome when giant monopolies and powerful concerns gain almost exclusive control of any field of enterprise so vital to the welfare of the people.
That is the outcome to which the government is deliberately exposing the consumers of Canada, if it pushes through this bill without offering any alternative protection to the retailer. But it is not only from the harmful effects of the increased power given to the giant concerns that the consumer will suffer. There is also an absolute lack of evidence that the consumer will benefit one iota from reduced prices as a result of the passage of the bill.
In that connection one can rely upon the evidence of Mr. McGregor who stated that in his opinion price maintenance was objectionable only because it is, as he described it, an undue restriction of competition-and not at all because of any effect it may have on

prices. In other words his opposition to the practice was based entirely upon his theory as to the forms of competition which should prevail in this country.
He was a knowledgeable witness; but if the evidence that Mr. McGregor's opposition to it was based entirely upon theory and not at all upon practical effects is not sufficient, then one need only refer to the evidence of the Prime Minister's position, as he stated it in the house yesterday, as found at page 2385 of Hansard:
I still do not think it will have very much effect on the cost of living index.
And so we find that the legislation is being rushed through on the basis of theory, on the theory of Mr. Fred McGregor and of the MacQuarrie committee, that the practice of resale price maintenance is an undue restriction of competition. For the purpose of serving these theoretical ideas, ideas that apparently are held by the government, the protection enjoyed by the retailer is to be removed, and the weak are to be allowed to die. For that is exactly the whole purport of Mr. McGregor's theory.
He said, "If there are retailers who will suffer as a result of the elimination of the practice of resale price maintenance-well, that is too bad. They probably were not efficient, anyway. And if they were not very efficient, then the community can get along without them, so let them be eliminated. Let them be extinguished. Let them die. The country can do without them." That is a most callous and a most unjustified attitude to take toward such a large and such a vital group in our country, one which has made so great a contribution to the strength of our economy.
It is difficult to avoid using strong words and harsh language when describing that outlook on the part of a theorist; but it is much more difficult to avoid using strong language to describe the situation which we now find, when that same point of view is expressed, not on the part of a theorist but on the part of this government, responsible as it is for the administration of affairs in this nation.
But that callous indifference to the fate of the small retailer is exactly the attitude reflected by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson); that is exactly the attitude reflected in this bill- that without any thought of consequence to the retailer, and without any recognition that the retailer has any interests to be preserved, this legislation, which is designed only to fulfil somebody's idea of a theory of free competition, should be rushed through, even if it eliminates the small retailer.

The evidence establishes that the small retailer needs the protection of resale price maintenance. At the present time it is his only protection against the powerful big interests. And let there be no mistake about it: the big interests are just as powerful and big in this day, just as crushing today, as they have been at any time in the history of this country. And the only protection retailers have built up for themselves, without any help from the government, is this method of doing business.
It is all nonsense to say that they wish it to be kept in private hands. If the government would study this matter, as we have urged it to do, and came forward with some alternative method by which the small retailer could be protected, he would be perfectly willing and indeed happy to give up his own system of protection, one which he has worked out and put into effect by himself.
But the government has not done that. They have refused to allow time for study and consideration which would be necessary to work out some alternative method. In the absence of that study, in the absence of that alternative protection, it can only be said that this legislation is being rushed through in an attitude of callous indifference to the welfare and the needs of the small retailer, and of the consuming public who will eventually, and before too long, as a result of this measure, be at the mercy of big, powerful monopolies, the chain and departmental stores.
The proof of what I am saying is found in the statement of the Prime Minister yesterday when, as set out at page 2385, he was attempting to justify the government's willingness to rush the small retailers of Canada into oblivion, and leave with a few big giants of industry the control of the distribution of goods in this country. He was referring to the possibility of the loss-leader practice. Well, I would ask the Prime Minister or, since he is not in his seat, the Minister of Justice, just how long he thinks it will take to consider and work out that recommendation? And at what stage

Combines Investigation Act will the government decide that it has become necessary to work out some alternative form of protection? How many retailers will have to go to the wall? How many bankruptcies will have to take place in Canada? How many small concerns will have to be taken over by the giants of the distributive trades before the government decides the time has come at which they must give consideration to some alternative form of protection for the small retailer? Section 1 of the bill proposes to write a new section 37A into the Combines Investigation Act. There are some difficulties as to its meaning that at once confront anyone reading this proposed section 37A. I draw your attention, first, to the fact that subsection 1 defines the word "dealer" in terms broad enough to include a manufacturer, a supplier or a vendor of an article. Subsection 2 purports to prohibit any act on the part of a dealer by threat, promise or agreement to induce or attempt to require any person to resell an article at a specified price under the named conditions. Subsection 3 purports to make it illegal for any dealer to refuse to sell or supply an article to any other person because that other person has refused to sell the article at prices as specified under the conditions named or has actually resold or offered for sale articles at prices less than those specified by the dealer.
I point out at once that there is nothing in the section dealing with the retailer. This section does not purport to deal with the act of the retailer in selling goods; it concerns itself only with the manufacturer or supplier of the goods who at an earlier stage has dealt with the retailer.
Combines Investigation Act
Some very serious questions are being asked throughout the merchandising trades of this country as to the effect of this section on a number of quite wholesome and natural commercial practices. At the present time many manufacturers and suppliers are getting out their seasonal catalogues for use in the new year. Many firms are supplying their representatives with these catalogues for their trips commencing with the beginning of the new year. This raises a very lively and urgent question. What is going to be the effect of this section on the current practice of naming prices in catalogues? Very often prices are suggested by the manufacturer or by the supplier who may be a wholesaler or a general jobber. He puts out a catalogue with retail prices named in it. These prices very often indicate what are con sidered in the view of the manufacturer, wholesaler or supplier to be reasonable prices for resale. It is not necessarily a case where any agreement is involved or any threat or inducement, but I am informed it is quite a general practice in the case of the printing of such catalogues. It seems to me that this becomes a pressing and urgent question and one of far-reaching importance affecting many of the merchandising trades in this country.
There is another question that has an important bearing. Probably it affects the pharmaceutical industry more than most of the others concerned. It is the practice, in the larger centres at any rate, for a good many of those operating pharmaceutical outlets, to unite in one large advertisement of articles that are under the system of resale price maintenance. If the system of resale price maintenance is to be made illegal now, what is to become of the practice, and a perfectly natural and quite proper practice it is, of pharmacists uniting in the publishing at their joint expense of large advertisements that would be beyond the means of any one of them? At the present time this is the only means that the smaller pharmaceutical outlets have for holding or trying to hold their own with the large outlets.
It is a very simple matter, as you will realize, Mr. Chairman, for the large departmental store or chain to take a whole page in a large city journal for the advertising of their sales or whatever it is in particular that they are featuring in the day's advertisement, but your small retailer cannot afford to go in for advertising on a scale of that kind. Therefore those interested in the same type of merchandise have in many cases made a practice of sharing the expensive advertisements of articles that they are

Combines Investigation Act all engaged in selling. Many of them are asking quite seriously and with a good deal of concern what is now to become of that practice. If it becomes illegal for them to join together in advertising articles for sale, the articles being sold at the same price in all their stores under the system of resale price maintenance, they are simply not going to be able to hold their own in the field of advertising.
Advertising is expensive, and small retailers cannot hope to compete when it comes to advertising. These are just two illustrations out of many that one could choose indicating the type of question that is very naturally and seriously troubling many retailers in this country. I have no doubt that this new section, if enacted, is going to be the subject of not a little judicial construction because of the complexity of the language used and the no little difficulty that one can see at a glance in its interpretation. These two instances I have singled out especially are troubling a great many people at the present time. I hope some statement can be made on behalf of the government to clarify the situation and to set clear limits on the effect of the proposed new section 37A, because if the offence to be created here is not defined in the clearest possible terms, and if its scope is not to be restricted so as not to include quite proper practices, then even more harm is going to be done than many of us see likely to follow from the bill.

does not have to adhere to the $3 if he does not wish to do so unless the manufacturer has set the $3 as a maximum price in which event not only can he fix the maximum price but he can also enforce it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Would that prevent the manufacturer from putting tags on the articles he sells indicating prices of $3, $4, $5, or whatever it may be?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: They can put their tags on as they are doing now?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Yes. For example take ladies hose of fine quality marketed in a container, and the suggested price is $2. That is quite all right but the manufacturer must not take any steps which could be regarded as an attempt to induce the retailer to sell at that price, and not less than that price.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: What about the position of an automobile or farm implement company which more or less compels the distributor to take a certain quantity at a certain price, and the agency is the sort of agency in which the retailer, if you like to call him such, does take the responsibility of buying and selling a quantity of goods and obtaining a certain amount of supplies for repairs and all the rest of it. Under this bill would the retailer be entitled to make his own arrangements regarding price or must he conform to the manufacturer's wishes because he is something of an agent for that manufacturer? It seems to me it is complicated, but I should like the minister to tell us what happens in that case.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I think I clearly understand the hon. member's question because he has explained it with his usual lucidity, but perhaps he will permit me to draw a distinction with respect to the type of agency about which he is speaking, the so-called agent who owns his own business and buys his goods from the manufacturer and then resells the goods belonging to the so-called agent. Actually, he is not an agent in the strict sense at all, but a dealer in those goods.
Before I go on to answer the question, 1 should like to contrast with that gentleman a man who is an agent for a manufacturer in the true sense of the word. He may own his place of business, but the goods which he handles belong to the manufacturer and continue to belong to the manufacturer until title passes from the manufacturer to the consumer. In the case of which my hon. friend speaks, this bill will provide, when it goes into effect, that that dealer will be free to resell at whatever price he sees fit, and no sanctions can be imposed upon him for doing
so. In the case of the man who is the agent in the real sense, of course he will have, by reason of the nature of his arrangement with the manufacturer, to be guided by the manufacturer as to what price shall be attached to the goods.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: There is just one point in that connection. In the instance which I had in mind, what happens if this dealer sells an automobile, we will say, at a price less than that at which the manufacturer says it should be sold, and the manufacturer says he is going to take the agency away from the dealer? What recourse has that dealer under those circumstances?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Under those circumstances the manufacturer would be committing an offence under this bill.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Surely you can hire and fire.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I shall deal with that point in just a moment. If the manufacturer refused a further supply to the dealer because the dealer had sold for less than the maintained price, the manufacturer would commit an offence under this bill.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: So that the bill gives some security to that dealer?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: It does indeed. If, however, as the hon. member for Wentworth has interjected, a question arises as to whether a man can hire and fire, I believe, if I understand the point he meant to make by his interjection, that the manufacturer should continue to have the right, notwithstanding the passage of this bill, of terminating an arrangement with the dealer which was unsatisfactory to the manufacturer for reasons other than the cutting of the suggested price. If, for example, because the dealer was intemperate and did not attend to business he became a poor credit risk, or if he maintained a slovenly establishment which was a poor advertisement for the manufacturer's product, or for a number of other reasons, there was legitimate cause for the manufacturer to terminate the arrangement according to its terms, then the termination would not be an offence under this proposed law.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Who would establish the measure of tidiness that must be maintained?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I mentioned that, but perhaps it is not a very good example.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I think it is excellent, because it just indicates the world of make-believe in which this whole thing is being discussed.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I shall be glad to discuss my hon. friend's point. If the manufacturer has a dealer who has failed or refused to sell the manufacturer's products at the suggested

Combines Investigation Act resale price and the manufacturer refuses to supply that dealer with renewal goods or takes any other action to force him into maintaining the suggested price, then the manufacturer would be guilty of an infraction of this legislation. If the manufacturer, however, took any action in relation to his dealer, such as the cancellation of his contract or the refusal to supply him with more goods, not because he had reduced the maintained price but for other good and lawful reasons, then the fact that the manufacturer has taken that action would not, of itself, be an offence under this proposed legislation. Whether or not the action of any manufacturer would fall in one category as offence under the act or as a lawful action under the contract would depend upon the evidence that was laid before the courts. The judge would have to decide that issue.
The hon. member may say that is all in the land of make-believe, but if that is so then almost every lawsuit that comes before the court involves questions of fact of much the same character. The judge has to decide whether the reason for the cancellation of the arrangement is the failure to maintain a price or whether it is some other valid cause of action. In actual practice I would not think there would be any great difficulty in a competent court reaching an opinion on a question of fact of that sort.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Would that apply if the dealer sold at a higher price instead of a lower price?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: No, it would not under this bill. I had better withdraw that answer and amplify it a bit to make it not only responsive to the question but also accurate. While the manufacturer cannot, under this bill, set a minimum price or a price below which the dealer may not sell, he can set a maximum price above which the dealer cannot sell. That maximum price which he can impose, he can enforce by whatever methods he may now be using to enforce resale price maintenance. In other words, in the legislation a provision is made that if a manufacturer wants to protect the consumer by assuring himself and the consumer that the consumer shall not have to pay more than a certain figure-we will say $5 for a hat-he can fix a maximum price of $5, and he can take whatever steps may be necessary to make that $5 resale price stick, that the dealer cannot sell for above that price; but if the dealer wants to, he can sell below it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: He can mark in the hat at the factory: This hat is to be sold for $5?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Surely.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I should like to ask the
minister a question which has been causing me concern as the debate has been proceeding. One of the things I want to be clear on is this. Suppose the manufacturer is selling regularly to a retailer one or more articles of merchandise in the usual course of business, that the retailer is purchasing from the manufacturer directly and is paying the manufacturer according to the pricing arrangements they have. Then suppose the manufacturer and the retailer decide that that relationship is going to be changed and that the retailer is no longer going to act in his independent capacity but will be the agent for the sale of those products of the manufacturer. Is it possible, under this legislation, for that change of relationship to take place? If it does, then of course, as I understand the bill, it comes outside the terms and provisions of this legislation.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
It will come outside the
provisions of the act itself provided that the arrangement, to which my hon. friend refers as an agency arrangement, is an agency arrangement in the strict sense; that is, in the sense that the dealer will give up his own identity in the control over his own business and enter into an arrangement with the manufacturer under which, to all intents and purposes, he will become an employee of the manufacturer doing as the manufacturer tells him to do, and under which the manufacturer will own the goods and direct him as to what he is to do. If that is the arrangement, then of course the principals in the contract of sale will no longer be the dealer and the consumer but will be the manufacturer and [DOT]the consumer, and the commercial identity of the former dealer will be lost entirely. He will be submerged in the identity of the manufacturer.
The reason why I rather emphasize that distinction is that there is a term that is quite commonly used; it is said that such and such a firm is the "exclusive agency" in such and such a city for such and such a product. I am under the impression that in [DOT]the majority of cases in which that arrangement is made, the so-called exclusive agency means nothing more than that the manufacturer sells goods to this dealer who buys [DOT]them, pays for them, owns them and as a principal himself resells them to the ultimate purchaser, and that the only basis for the term "exclusive agency" is that that manufacturer chooses to deal with that particular dealer because he is a man of repute and of reputation in the community, and the manufacturer has goods of a high quality and

wants to deal with a high-quality representative. But he is not an agent in the sense in which I think my hon. friend was using the term.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: My point was this, if I may extend it a step further. I did not have in mind that the retailer would be the employee, for instance, of the manufacturer. I had in mind that he might perhaps be an agent, that the goods might be sent on consignment to the retailer and that a commission would be charged by the retailer upon the sale when it was made. The goods, I take it, would then of course be at the risk of the manufacturer until the title had passed to the ultimate purchaser. But if that is the case- and this is the reason I raised the question- it looks as though if any manufacturer decided to adopt that course of creating a bona fide agency arrangement between the retailer and himself, this act would be of no avail whatsoever in the protection either of the consumer or of business generally. If that were to be done on a broad-scale basis, this act would be just so much eyewash from the point of view of protecting those parts of our business that the minister has in mind giving protection to. That is the point I wanted to be made clear upon because it seems to me that if you are going to have an act it ought to have some powers and it ought to have reasonably wide coverage or else not be brought in at all. But if what I have suggested is the case, I can see exactly what is apt to happen-as can the minister and everybody in the committee who has some relation to business-namely, that you are going to find that the people the minister is trying to take a crack at in this legislation are not going to be there when he cracks the whip. That is the position I should like to be made clear on.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
With great deference, Mr. Chairman, I must say that I do not entirely share my hon. friend's apprehensions in that regard. He knows as well as we all do that at the present time we have, under the present system of resale price maintenance, a large number of these business concerns in which, the manufacturer retains control of his product until it is sold to the consumer. You find that situation in the clothing trade, the candy trade and in a number of others. In that case the manufacturer has made a decision that he, as a manufacturer, can take on the secondary function as a distributor and that he, in his capacity as a distributor, can distribute his own goods more satisfactorily and more economically for himself than he can by selling them to the trade. The independent retailers and the independent wholesalers of the country are facing that kind of 94699-1561
Combines Investigation Act competition right at the present time in all of these fields. I do not think for a moment that the passage of this bill will alter to any substantial extent that competition that now exists; but I should have thought that the decision of the manufacturer to enter into the distributive trade would probably be inspired or affected to a far greater extent by other considerations than by the passage of this bill. If up until the present time he has not felt that there was any particular advantage to him to get into the distributive business, I do not think that the passage of this bill is going to drive him there. For that reason I do not share my hon. friend's apprehension. I think the point that he makes is a colourable one, shall I say; there is point to my hon. friend's remarks. But I think that we will find that there will be no great increase in the fairly substantial amount of manufacturer distribution which is being carried on at the present time. I do not think that will likely change because that is very well established, as my hon. friend knows, in most of these cases like the Laura Secord people and the Tip Top Tailors and so on.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Before the discussion goes too far afield, will the minister come back to the other question I asked him originally in regard to the joint advertising project carried out by the retailers selling the same type of product?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I will be glad to do so, but I was going to say with some reluctance. I guess there is an inconsistency there. I am a little bit reluctant to do it for this reason. I do not know whether the hon. member for Eglinton was in the chamber when I was asked questions during the debate on second reading on this very point, but the hon. member for York South-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Yes, I was present. His question was similar to the questions I have asked.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That is correct. Perhaps my hon. friend will recall that I asked a counter question as to just what it was that was done before this advertisement was put in the newspaper. Did the gentlemen who got together each week to draft this advertisement agree as to the contents of the advertisement, or did they agree as to the price of the articles that were advertised in the advertisement, because if they agreed-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I will clear that up. These articles in the given case I take it are all price-maintained. Here is a group of retailers who are selling the same group of articles, in each case at the same price. They are not fixing the price, they are simply following or applying the policy of price-maintenance, laid down by the manufacturer. In their case,

Combines Investigation Act what is going to become of these advertisements? Are they going to be denied any opportunity of sharing together in advertisements of the same articles, as they are doing at the present time. A joint advertisement is the only way in which numbers of these smaller retailers can hope to compete with the big full-page advertisements of the larger retail outlets.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I appreciate the manner in which my hon. friend has elucidated this point, but he has hardly met my difficulty completely, I think, for this reason. A case of this sort, as I am sure my hon. friend as a lawyer would agree, depends to a very large extent indeed upon the facts. What my hon. friend is asking for really is a legal opinion as to what effect this legislation would have upon a certain practice which he says is being followed. If I say that it will have no effect, and then it turns out that my hon. friend's information as to just what is done at these meetings is inaccurate, it would be very difficult for me to convince anyone afterwards that I gave advice upon a certain set of facts, and the real facts were different from those which he had represented to me. In saying this I am not questioning his veracity; not for a moment. Perhaps I can answer his question in this way. If in fact these gentlemen at these meetings at which the text of the advertisement is agreed upon did reach an agreement as to prices, then that, I apprehend, would be unlawful not under this new amendment but under the existing Combines Investigation Act, provided that it was significantly preventing competition to the public detriment.
If, on the other hand-this is the case that my hon. friend poses-these prices were maintained prices which have been up until the present time quite legal-I understand that is what he contends-and that the advertisement advertises such maintained prices, then the passage of this legislation would make it impossible to advertise maintained prices because maintained prices themselves are made illegal by the bill.
Whether or not what my hon. friend has stated-and what I am stating by way of reply-is in accordance with the actual facts of the case, I am not in a position to say, and I would very much prefer that no person should take this exchange between my hon. friend and myself too seriously until we get the actual facts of the case before us and express an opinion concerning them.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That warning is unnecessary.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: This is an extraordinary procedure. The Minister of Justice has said: Now, I have made an answer, but do not let anybody think I am bound by it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: We are not asking free legal advice from the Minister of Justice; we are asking for the government's interpretation of this legislation. I prefaced what I had to say on this subject by indicating that so far as my reading of this section is concerned, it just abounds with difficulties as to its meaning. It seems to me that this is a section that, when it is submitted to judicial interpretation, is going to present very great difficulties. That is why I think we wish to understand now just what it is we are dealing with. The case that I put before the minister was put for illustration. I think that he has in his answer introduced all the qualifications, surely, and all the statements of pertinent facts that are relevant to his answer. But I think when he does qualify his answer to his heart's content or introduces all kinds of hypothetical circumstances, surely when his answer is given we are entitled to understand that that is a considered answer and the government's view as to the effect of this legislation. I emphasize again, this is not an idle question.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: On a question of privilege, before my hon. friend goes away from this point, I should like to make it clear, if I have not already done so, that I have tried, and I think successfully, to give an answer to the set of facts which my hon. friend has posed as the basis for his question; and I am quite willing to be accountable for that answer to his set of facts. But what I have suggested, with all respect, and not in any way questioning his veracity, is that it may well be that the real facts are not as he imagines them to be. I am simply uttering a note of warning that to the extent that the real facts are different from those which he has suggested, then to that extent my answer will not apply to the real facts. In other words, I do not want my hon. friend, nor do I want the Drug Trading Company, or whatever the organization is, to say, on the basis of the answer I have given to the facts stated by my hon. friend that, well, we are out in the clear on the basis of the real facts; but if the real facts are as stated by my hon. friend-and they may very well be-then I stand right behind my answer.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I do not think anyone would ever propose to hold the minister to an answer except in terms of the question, and the question in this case is surrounded by

what I thought was an ample statement of the understood facts. Certainly, the minister has predicated his answer upon the correctness of the facts as stated. Indeed, he has gone further and introduced a number of qualifications and hypotheses that surely qualify his answer to his own satisfaction. That answer having been given, I think the committee is entitled to feel that it is a considered answer; that it is the government's understanding of the legislation that it is introducing, and that it is its legislative purpose in connection with this measure.
I think this question must be considered further. This is not an idle question; this is a very serious matter for a great many retailers because, as I have indicated to you, the only way in which they can hope to compete in advertising with the large retail outlets is by association together, pooling *the expense of advertisements.
Now, we are told on the one hand that if today they are going out to fix prices by a combination among themselves in a manner detrimental to the public interest, that is already contrary to the act. And we are told on the other hand that if this is not that case, but is simply a case of resale price-maintenance, laid down by the manufacturer who supplies these goods to all retailers, on these or similar terms, for sale at the maintained price, such practice is to become illegal.
But that is not the end of the question. The manufacturer is quite at liberty to indicate the maximum price. We have already been told that he is at liberty to suggest what he considers a fair price, so long as he does not attempt to lay down sanctions as applied to anyone who does not choose to follow his view as to fair price. But what is to be the position of a group of retailers in the same business who, in the light of a maximum price indicated by the manufacturer or a fair price suggested by the manufacturer, choose to unite together in publishing an advertisement which says, for instance, that the John Jones tooth brush is to be offered for sale at an indicated number of pharmaceutical outlets at a price of fifty cents, and that, we will say, a particular type of toothpaste is available at that group of pharmaceutical outlets at a price of forty-nine cents? There may be a dozen other articles in the same advertisement.
This is a very important question. It is something that agitates pharmacists and merchants who are motivated in their business dealings by the highest purposes. Their operations are honourable and above reproach. They keep within the law. They
Combines Investigation Act obey the law, and they wish to continue to do so. At the same time they do not wish to be exposed to the ravages of unfair competition at the hands of big and powerful retail outlets.
In the case I have put before the minister, I do not think we have had by any means an adequate answer to the question. Assuming that this legislation passes, what is the position with respect to the desire of those retailers who are interested in the same type of commodity to associate themselves in a common advertisement?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Following up the same question, I should like to ask the minister if I understood him to imply that the joint advertising done in the past by groups of independent retailers or by voluntary chains contravenes the Combines Investigation Act. Also, whether they did or not, and if there is any question at all as to the legality of the joint advertising, who will be guilty? Will the retailers themselves be the ones charged, or will the newspapers be deemed guilty by reason of having published these advertisements?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the question asked by the hon. member for Hamilton West is pretty good proof of the difficulty which arises in reply to questions such as that asked by the hon. member for Eglinton. The substance of the question of the hon. member for Eglinton was this: Can these druggists continue to advertise maintained prices? My answer was that since resale price maintenance will be banned by this legislation, it will be impossible to advertise maintained prices. That is my answer.
I did not say that they could not have joint advertising, which is a different question entirely. The difficulty arises in a matter of this kind, as any lawyer with any experience, such as that of the hon. member for Eglinton, will tell you, that the first thing counsel wants to know when asked for an opinion is this: What are the facts of this case? He wants to know what the real facts are-not the hypothetical ones, but the real ones. He will not give an opinion until he is told the facts clearly.
If the hon. member for Hamilton West has a different set of facts in mind, that there are not going to be maintained prices in some other type of advertising, then that indicates another answer.
My point is that this sort of question and answer procedure in committee is more likely to create misunderstanding than to illuminate the subject. One cannot express an opinion until he knows exactly what it is

Combines Investigation Act that these gentlemen propose to do. We are doing these men a disservice until we can consult with them and find out what it is they have in mind to do alter the act is passed. Then we can tell whether they will be acting in compliance with the act.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I think it is fairly obvious that what they want to do is to proceed in the manner in which they have in the past.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I should like to ask the
minister whether it was his intention to indicate that this joint advertising has in the past run contrary to the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act. I gathered that from some of his remarks. I wonder now just what happens to this group of retailers. They are probably a voluntary chain-and I presume the minister understands that when I refer to a voluntary chain I mean that each store is independently owned and that they group together for purposes of identification. Each person, however, is the owner of his own store, and his association with other members is purely voluntary. In the past they have published advertisements jointly. Of course they would have to agree on the prices which would go in those advertisements. They would have to agree, because the very fact that they put their names to the advertisement would mean that they agreed.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
No. Perhaps my hon. friend
would permit me to interrupt. I think this would be an excellent interruption, if I may be permitted to say so. I assume that they do not agree at all. But if not, were they not advertising drug prices-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Not necessarily at all.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Just a moment, now. Were
they not advertising drug prices which had been fixed at the manufacturing level by resale price maintenance?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: He is trying to help you.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Because if they did not, if
they got together among themselves to fix prices as a horizontal combine, then that would be in contravention of the act-not this present bill, but the act itself. That would be so, provided competition was eliminated to some extent by their action in so doing.
So their problem, it seems to me, is this- and these are not the best auspices under which to discuss it-their problem has been that under a system of lawful resale price maintenance, under which manufacturers

have fixed resale prices of these products, they could publish joint advertisements. Having regard to the fact that resale price maintenance is lawful, and that it is lawful to advertise, the advertisement would be quite all right.
But now the question arises as asked by the hon. member for Eglinton: If we ban resale price maintenance, can they continue to do that? And of course if we ban maintained prices, the presumption arises at once that they have agreed to fix the prices themselves. Perhaps I would illuminate the subject a little more if I were to put it this way-although this perhaps is a ridiculous supposition: Let us suppose that these gentlemen pool their resources in advertising. From what the hon. member has said, I understand that they are all independent. If their prices were not the same on different products, there would be no question at all, because there would be no suggestion or thought of their being the same.
