If they do so and do it to the extent that it is contrary to public interest by a significant reduction in competition, then that would be an offence under the act. I assume that up until the present time they have just been advertising resale-maintained prices?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That is not the fact and that is not what I meant. I take it from what the minister has now said that it is quite legal for A and P or Loblaw's or Dominion Stores to publish full-page advertisements indicating that you can buy ketchup in any store for twenty-seven cents, but it would be against the law apparently for a chain composed of independent merchants to publish the same advertisement and say that you could buy ketchup at any of their stores for twenty-seven cents. That would be considered collusion.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: He did not say that.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That is what it sounded like to me.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: This just illustrates-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: The stupidity of the legislation.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: No. It just illustrates the difficulty of trying to give a legal opinion upon a set of facts asked by the hon. member for Eglinton, and again upon a somewhat different set of facts asked by the hon. member for Hamilton West, and so on.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: They are simple facts.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I think an exchange of this sort is doing a disservice to all concerned.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: These are the very things that are bothering merchants. I cannot see that it is doing a disservice to try to clarify the situation; quite the contrary. As a matter of fact, I was not talking about price-maintained articles entirely because a great many of the products and articles which are advertised jointly are not price-maintained nor have they ever been price-maintained. That is particularly true of food items. You see these big advertisements in the paper every Thursday where the chains advertise prices which will be in effect in their stores for the weekend buying. I asked the minister before whether that advertising would be contrary to the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act in the past.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: If it is against public interest only.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: It does not matter whether they contravene the act or not, it is not a matter of whether it is against public interest or not; I would say that that is secondary. The question is whether one set of dealers or one dealer operating through a number of outlets can practise a certain advertising policy while another group which has chained together cannot.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: May I point out to the minister that I think that he has quite overlooked an important feature of this bill. The question has to do with something done or undertaken by retailers. There is nothing in this bill that says anything about retailers. The proposed section 37A does not deal with acts done by retailers.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: They are included in the definition.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: The definition of the word "dealer" is broad enough to include someone who sells goods, but look at subsections 2 and 3 and you will see that there is nothing there that applies to what is done by retailers.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: My friend's question concerned retailers.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That is my point and for that reason I think the minister's answer is in error. I think in undertaking to answer these questions he has completely overlooked the fact that this bill has no application to acts by retailers. It purports to apply only to those who are supplying or selling to retailers.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Has my hon. friend looked at the definition of "dealer"?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I referred to the definition of "dealer" when I opened my remarks this afternoon and just now. It is quite true that the word "dealer" is defined in terms broad
Combines Investigation Act enough to include a manufacturer, a supplier or a vendor. But look at the operative terms of section 37A; look at subsection 2. There is nothing there that applies to an act of a retailer selling to a consumer. There is nothing in the bill that applies to that situation. I think the answer of the minister is in error.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: The minister's answer referred to the case of retailers combining together which would be illegal under the existing act, not under the amendment.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
That was only one fragment of the minister's answer. He dealt with the situation that exists before this bill comes into effect. Whatever may be said about the correctness of his interpretation, certainly that has to be dealt with in the terms of the present legislation. The other question was as to the effect of this legislation on practices that exist. The minister has given a long answer which I think in the light of a proper reading of this section is quite erroneous.
This illustrates the importance of insisting on a discussion of this kind in committee. After all, what is a committee stage for except to probe into the terms of legislation like this and try to find out what they mean. Let us turn the sections inside out and see what they mean. We have been discussing this section for less than an hour and it seems to me that it is already apparent that the government does not understand the full extent of this legislation or what is involved and what is not involved in it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I should like to follow up this matter of advertising with the minister. I understand that a firm like Loblaw's can publish a full-page advertisement in the Toronto papers indicating that certain items can be bought in any one of fifteen or twenty Loblaw stores in Toronto and suburbs at a given price. What we are trying to find out is what would be involved if an association like the independent druggists or the independent grocery alliance, each of which has a number of stores, get together and publish a joint advertisement and name the prices at which items may be purchased in each of their stores. Is that just as lawful as if Dominion Stores, A and P or some other chain did the same thing?
Here is a full-page advertisement indicating what I have in mind. This appeared in the Toronto papers, and similar advertisements appear many times through the week. A number of stores combine, and apparently there is no violation under the present act, or there has been no indication that there
2466	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act is a violation. Some of the articles advertised are price-maintained, others are not. This has been going on for years. Will they still be permitted to publish these advertisements indicating the prices at which given articles can be bought in any of their stores?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I shall make another attempt to make myself clear in this matter. There is nothing to prevent a group publishing a joint advertisement, but in practice that advertisement-I am not suggesting this about that particular group of people-and the business of getting together to agree upon prices that are to be published may be merely a cloak for a horizontal price-fixing agreement. If that were the case, if it were a cloak and they were really fixing prices, the mere fact that under the law they have a perfectly lawful right to join together to publish a common advertisement would be no protection for them if it could be established that they had fixed prices. If the crown were able to prove in a given case that fixing went on to the extent of seriously interfering with competition, and that is what we would have to prove in order to prove that it was contrary to public interest, that would result in a conviction. But if a group of men came together and in good faith published a joint advertisement of prices of goods that were not resale price maintained, and if we can all imagine that by the most extraordinary coincidence they all happened to have individually the same price for the same article in the advertisement, if those were the facts then it would be quite within their rights to have a joint advertisement provided they were not using it as a means of fixing prices in contravention of the act. My hon. friend may say that all that sounds extremely complicated. In any practical case that would arise, we will say for prosecution, it would be a question of fact for the court to decide whether this was a bona fide coming together in a joint advertisement or whether on the facts of the case there had been a contravention of the act. My difficulty in discussing this question is that I am being asked, upon a purely hypothetical set of facts, to anticipate what judgment a court would give upon them.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Will the minister show me what is the difference, so far as interfering with competition is concerned, when fifteen or twenty Loblaw stores scattered throughout Toronto and suburbs advertise a set price for every given article on their shelves in stores that have different overheads and staffs and where the cost of doing business is different? Loblaw's, because they are one firm, can have fifty stores and fix prices for every one of their stores, and you say it does not interfere with competition.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
They are not conspiring with anybody else.
Mr. Nose worthy: If fifty independent dealers agree to advertise their prices that is interfering with competition and I should like to know what the difference is.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Loblaw's are all alone.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
When as a matter of policy in a country-for example, the United1 States, Canada or Great Britain which is now engaged in the task-it is decided to pass anti-trust or anti-combine legislation, they prohibit agreements reached between different concerns for the purpose of fixing prices over the whole field, or a significant part of the whole field, so as to achieve by that means the economic equivalent of a monopoly. When you prohibit an agreement, it is an agreement amongst various separate owners and proprietors of businesses. In the case that my hon. friend poses, while Loblaw's may operate twenty stores they are, as he well knows, all under one management. That management establishes the pricing for those stores but it does not establish it for the whole industry. They are subject to the competition not only of other chains and departmental stores but of all these other fifty retailers, thousands of other retailers, in that business.
If you say, by this ingenious point which my hon. friend has raised, that you are going to let groups of other people set prices by agreement, the practical question arises in the administration of legislation of this character as to just where you are going to draw the line. You have either got to prohibit price fixing agreements across the board or not prohibit them. If you do not prohibit them, then what happens, as has happened in certain industries which I will not name, is that everybody in the industry, at the retail level, the jobber's level and the manufacturer's level, gets together in one great arrangement that controls the price of the product from the time it is manufactured through all its stages until it reaches the consumer.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Would that not be an offence now under the Combines Investigation Act?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: For all who get together?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Would that not be an offence now if they all got together?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Oh yes, it surely would be. It is an offence if they all get together, and it is an offence if less than all get together.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: You said all.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
It would be an offence if the retailers got together in a horizontal agreement. It is an offence for the wholesalers

to get together in a common agreement. It is an offence for the manufacturers to get together, and if the whole bunch of them get together it is perhaps a more grave offence but it is still just an offence under the act. The difficulty which my hon. friend raises is one which arises out of the nature of legislation of this character. You are either going to prohibit price fixing agreements or you are not.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That is the character of the combines act, and all of this discussion for the past fifteen minutes has nothing to do with the bill. It has been on the combines act itself.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I understand it will be illegal for the 400 independent stores that form this voluntary group to get together, fix prices and advertise uniform prices. Yet it would be quite legal for these 400 stores to organize themselves into a corporation with one management and for that one management to fix the prices for the 400 stores.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That is what it encourages.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That is what you are encouraging. Is that not so?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Am I correct in that assumption?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: What is involved there is the surrender of the independence of every one of these proprietors to a larger concern. I think my hon. friend is right to this extent, that in dealing with arriving at agreements in contravention of the act you have to treat each proprietor, large and small, as an entity whose consent is a necessary feature in any agreement that he may reach with others to fix prices in contravention of the act. My hon. friend is quite right that it does not make any difference whether it is a large or small dealer. He acts as an individual and his consent is necessary to arriving at that agreement.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I think this bill is very confusing to a great many retailers. I have had considerable correspondence with executive members of the Canadian farm implement retailers association. You have partly cleared up the difficulty with the reference to the automobile agency or large farm implement agency that may lose its contract. I think the majority of the larger farm implements are handled on a catalogue basis. The prices are set out every year by the larger companies not only for their machines but for parts and repairs. In many cases that I know of a genuine agent handles these farm implements. He sets up an 94699-157
Combines Investigation Act organization by agreement with a company to service the implements over a term of years. He purchases his own property and in many cases he purchases the parts outright from the particular company and carries on that service. These people are quite worried as to whether or not the legislation will interfere with them. Every time they go to their shelves for a particular part they look up the catalogue put out by the farm implement company concerned and charge their customers on the basis of the catalogue price. They are very much concerned as to whether the legislation will interfere with their carrying on on that basis. As I interpret it, that is really price maintenance.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: When my hon. friend asks whether or not it interferes, what does he mean?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Is it price maintenance? The minister pointed out to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that a person could lose his agency for not carrying out the instructions of the company, and would come under this new legislation. Supposing someone comes along and reports one of those men carrying on this service. There is an investigation, and the dealer finds he is in difficulty for not adhering to this catalogue price. Is that considered as interference under this legislation?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I am not sure that I understand the hon. member's point. Perhaps I had better restate it and he can take careful note to make sure that I am stating his point correctly. If at the present time the basis upon which the implement dealer gets his implements and repair parts from the manufacturer is that in reselling them he must charge the customer the prices that are set out in the catalogue or else he will lose his agency or have some form of punishment imposed upon him-is it the hon. member's view that is the situation?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I am told it is not a hard and fast contract, but it is a suggested price. Nevertheless, I do know what has happened in many cases where the dealer has deviated from that suggested price.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: The manufacturer has withdrawn the agency?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That has happened in some cases.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
The effect of this bill will be that the dealer who purchased his implements or repair parts from the manufacturer and has paid for them, will have title to those implements. If he wishes he can sell them at the suggested price in the catalogue to which my hon. friend refers, but if he wishes to

Combines Investigation Act sell them for less than that the manufacturer cannot do anything to him, as the hon. member says he is doing now.
If the hon. member regards the penalties which are now imposed on the dealer as objectionable in any way, then this bill will do away with those penalties.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Getting back to what we were discussing before the member for Souris spoke, it is obvious that the large grocery chains like A & P or Loblaw's can combine their advertising for all their stores, and therefore can afford to advertise the products sold at all their stores, at whatever prices they want. The small stores cannot afford to advertise singly, and that is why, in the past, they have combined in order to make it possible to advertise their goods and draw customers to their stores. In the future, in order to compete with these large chain stores, there will be great compulsion on them to merge together in order to advertise and maintain stable prices. This eliminates individual competition; and will mean that you are only going to have mergers of small units, and you are going to do away with the individual unit. Does the minister agree that is what this legislation will make it almost impossible to get away from?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
No; I do not agree with that at all, Mr. Chairman. It seems to me there has been considerable confusion of thought between the provisions of this bill, on the one hand, and the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act on the other. When I am asked to say what would happen on the basis of a certain set of facts, and to those facts the existing Combines Investigation Act is perhaps more applicable than this bill, I think in all honesty I have to give an answer in terms of the existing Combines Investigation Act.
Perhaps I could make this whole difficulty over advertising more clear if I put it in this way. It is now legal, and will continue to be legal after this bill is passed, to advertise all non-price-maintained goods which would include most of the groceries and will include nearly all goods after the bill comes into effect. I think I had better stop there, because that will leave a clearer impression in the minds of the members concerning the difficulty we have been discussing. It is a difficulty which does not arise under this bill at all, but is a difficulty under the Combines Investigation Act in its present form.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That is not an answer to my question at all.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Perhaps we can clarify it. The trouble is that everyone is asking questions and getting different answers to the same

questions; that is what is bothering me. I am very unhappy about the answer that was given to the member for York South.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: A new assistant.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I do not know why there is all the shouting. You are trying to get an interpretation of an act, and I am not giving legal advice. I want to understand what this means. I shall give the minister a set of facts to see if I understand the bill. A, B, C and D are retailers who buy from manufacturer X. The suggested retail price is 10 cents. They all advertise the article at 10 cents in a joint advertisement. Under this bill is there anything illegal about that transaction?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Under the present bill?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: The present bill has nothing at all to do with it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: A suggestion has been made that 300 or 400 retail stores might combine in order to obtain the same results as Loblaw's and A & P. The thought occurs to me that the only way that could be done would be for one company to buy out these 300 or 400 stores.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: If these stores were run the same as Loblaw's, the managers and clerks would be on a salary. The stores would be united, and you would have exactly the same circumstances as those under which Loblaw's operate. But if the 400 grocers got together and decided they would form a combine-that is the suggestion here-and said they would come under the one head but run under their own businesses and just get together on price, then that would be a combine.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: No, a merger.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: No, it is a combine. If it is not under one management and the managers are not on a salary, then it is a combine.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I want to follow up the question put by the hon. member for Souris. Supposing a manufacturer discontinued supplying a retailer without giving any reason whatever, or ostensibly for some reason other than cutting price, what is there in this bill to prevent that? Supposing a co-operative society wishes to buy a line of implements: can a manufacturer refuse to supply the dealer in the one instance or the co-operative in the other instance with that line of goods? Is there anything in this bill or in the Combines

Investigation Act which would enable either the dealer under those circumstances or an organized co-operative to get a line of goods such as implements, for example-that is perhaps what we are most interested in at the moment-without any discrimination whatsoever?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I would refer my hon. friend, if he has the bill there, to subsection 3.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I have read that.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
It reads as follows:
No dealer shall refuse to sell or supply an article or commodity to any other person for the reason that such other person
(a) has refused to resell or to offer for resale the article or commodity
(i)	at a price specified by the dealer or established by agreement,
(ii)	at a price not less than a minimum price specified by the dealer or established by agreement,
(iii)	at a markup or discount specified by the dealer or established by agreement,
(iv)	at a markup not less than a minimum markup specified by the dealer, or established by agreement, or
(v)	at a discount not greater than a maximum discount specified by the dealer or established by agreement . . .
In other words, if the retailer has broken the price by selling for less, and the manufacturer subsequently refuses renewal of supplies or cancels the contract of supply, then I imagine what would happen is that a complaint would be made to the combines investigation branch, and we would inquire into the circumstances. If they revealed what seemed to be a case against the manufacturer, a charge would be laid; and when that was tried, the question of fact would be for the court to decide on the evidence as to whether the manufacturer, in refusing renewal supplies or in cancelling the arrangement with the dealer, did so in contravention of this section or whether he had other good reasons for doing so. If he had no other good reasons, and if the man was the same credit risk that he had always been and was doing a good job in every way, I should think that the conclusion which it would be almost irresistible for the court to come to would be that the real reason for the cancellation of the contract or the refusal for renewal of supplies was the fact that the price had been broken.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Having read that particular part of the bill, I had come to the conclusion that this rather restricted the grounds upon which a manufacturer could refuse to sell. It seemed to me that if we are really trying to bring about competition and to end this particular practice, we should simply have this clause read in this way:
94699-157J
Combines Investigation Act
"No dealer shall refuse to sell or supply an article or commodity to another person."
It seemed to me that we should stop there. Then every co-operative could obtain goods and every dealer could obtain goods; and once he obtained the goods and bought the goods, he could sell the goods in any way he liked. It seems to me that the clause should stop there if that is the intent of the bill.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: With all deference, Mr. Chairman, I think that my hon. friend has not given his last suggestion the careful consideration and good judgment that he usually gives to matters that come before the House of Commons; because if we made it the law that any manufacturer would have to sell goods to any person-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Who would pay for them.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: -who would pay for them, I would think that would be quite an extreme interference with the freedom of the individual, and much more so than anything that is contemplated in the whole of the act at the present time.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I have listened to the Minister of Justice, and I think he ought to pay a compliment to the hon. member for Spadina for applying a little bit of the common sense to which the Minister of Justice referred yesterday when he himself was discussing these sections. I do not know where we would have been but for the hon. member for Spadina and the assistance of the combines commissioner, although not on the floor of the house.
As to the present section, the point raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is clear. The Minister of Justice seems to forget that with regard to prosecutions there is such a rule as that intent must be established; and the intent is fully set out in this section which says:
No dealer shall refuse to sell or supply an article or commodity to any other person for the reason that such other person
(a) has refused to resell or to offer for resale the article or commodity
(i) at a price specified by the dealer or established by agreement . . .
And so on. My hon. friend says that it is a question of fact. Certainly it is a question of fact that can only be determined if there is evidence upon which a court could determine it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
On the statement made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar there is no authority under this act that will deny the right of any dealer simply to refuse to deliver any commodity, whatever it may

Combines Investigation Act be, as long as the reason is not given. That point indicates exactly how half-baked legislation comes before the House of Commons, without the care and the attention it should receive. While the endeavour has been to close the door, in fact the door has been opened. There is no onus upon the accused. The crown must prove, in the prosecution, that the dealer refused to sell or supply the article or commodity for the reason that the intended purchaser has refused to be bound by the resale price.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: The hon. member said: If the reason is not mentioned.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Even if the reason is not mentioned for the refusal to supply goods, does the hon. member, who is a lawyer, not realize that the reason can be established by outside evidence?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That is, by collateral evidence.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Of the circumstances.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That is true.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: It does not have to be mentioned in the act.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That is simply an interruption that is meaningless.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I beg your pardon. It contradicts what you were saying.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That is true.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: It is not meaningless for that reason, surely.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
No; it is not meaningless to my hon. friend. But the point I am making is this, Mr. Chairman. By the section itself imposing the onus on the prosecution, the situation to which I have referred is possible, provided that there are no documents to the contrary or that there is no evidence to the contrary. If there is evidence, as my hon. friend says, then it will be established that the reason for refusal to deal was the refusal of the intended purchaser to resell at the resale price; that is so if there is evidence, either direct or circumstantial. But circumstantial evidence is certainly far different from what was referred to a moment ago as a principle by the Minister of Justice when he says that the courts may come to a conclusion as a fact that the reason for the

denial was the fact that the purchaser refused to be bound. There would have to be some evidence of that, either direct or circumstantial, as the hon member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine has said.
For two days the Minister of Justice has been telling the house how difficult it is to get convictions under the Combines Investigation Act. In the United States it takes three years to get the evidence. If this section is passed as it now stands, and an alteration is not made in the draft, there is no reason why any person in this country need fear prosecution. I refer particularly to implement manufacturers or distributors, automobile distributors and the like. I take those as examples. Under the law as we intend to pass it, if it goes through in its present form, the crown will have an impossible task in proving intent; for, as the Minister of Justice has repeatedly said, prospective wrongdoers do not leave any more traces or fingerprints than they can help. He pointed out yesterday, with such power and force, that these great corporations have outstanding lawyers to act for them. That was given as an excuse for the fact that in some of the prosecutions government counsel were less astute than they ought to have been in the prosecution, and in the results of prosecutions no doubt. The fact remains that under the section as it now stands the onus on the prosecution would allow every manufacturer in this country, without giving any reasons- he need give no reasons-to simply say: On and after a certain date I do not wish to supply you. If there is no more than that available, and no circumstantial evidence, as the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine mentions, then there can be no conviction. I also point out that under this legislation there is nothing that will deny any manufacturer the right to say that one prospective purchaser shall be on a quota, and one quota shall be small and another large.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: And that it will be six weeks before you get your order.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
There is nothing to indicate that any offence will be committed if a dealer simply says: On and after this date, for no reason-and they will certainly set forth in the letter; we have no reason for doing this-your quota will be such and such. I point that out as a second weakness in the draft section.
As I see them, these two weaknesses can have the effect of parliament passing the section in its present form and constituting a threat, and effective in so far as commodities now on the shelves of the retailers are concerned, but ineffective as against any future

dealings that might take place. In its present form, as I see it, the section will be-and I repeat-ineffective in relation to the various retailers who have goods in stock. They will be able to sell them; but in so far as goods that are in the wholesalers' stocks today are concerned, and which will ultimately find their way into the possession of the retailer, the section as it now stands will, in my opinion, come within the ambit of Colonel Ralston's description of section 498A in 1936 when he used the scriptural words, a sham and a delusion. Certainly-and I am not going into the question of loss leaders at the moment, although I hope the opportunity does come before we conclude the discussion on this section-in its present form the onus is on the prosecution, provided that the manufacturer or the distributor does not openly advertise the fact that he is refusing to sell because of his belief or his knowledge that the intended purchaser is not maintaining the price; and he will have nothing to fear as regards commodities that have not yet been bargained for or delivered. I place this before the minister with some knowledge of what proof is needed in the courts and some knowledge of combines cases from both sides, prosecution and defence.
If the minister does desire to do more than use a smokescreen in order to delude people into believing that something effective is being done, then section 37A will have to be revamped in order to assure that too great an onus is not placed upon the crown. I think that subsection 3 (a) and (b) will have to be redrawn, otherwise the crown itself will be establishing in law what the onus must be. In my opinion, with proper defence, it would be most difficult if not impossible to secure a conviction for goods that are to be bargained for after the date on which this legislation comes into effect. I bring that to the minister's attention. He may say that it has been considered by the law officers of the crown. That does not in any way deter me from offering suggestions. The law officers of the crown have drawn many laws, and they have been passed by parliament, and on the first occasion that they have found their way into the courts for interpretation, judges who are in no way affected by sentiment or considerations such as that, determining the law, as it has to be determined, by what parliament passes, will not consider what has been said in parliament in determining the degree of the onus or the need of requisite proof in order to establish and discharge that onus.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I think I should make a brief reply to my hon. friend and say that we are greatly indebted to get from him the opinion of a man who, as he has correctly stated,
Combines Investigation Act has had a great deal of experience in criminal law and in connection with the present act. I am glad to have this opinion. But it so happens that we have also had the opinions not only from the law officers of the crown to whom he referred, but from experienced officers who have had long years of work with the Combines Investigation Act.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Who are they?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: One of them is Mr. Whiteley, who has been with the department for many years, and another one is Mr. MacDonald, who is a former deputy attorney general of Nova Scotia, and who has been with the department for about three years, and a number of others besides. They do not happen to share the opinion which has just been expressed by my hon. friend, and I must say for my own part that I would be much more impressed with his opinion if he would just go on and state the text that he would suggest to tighten up the hole that he says is now in this section. If he cannot get his criticism down to more definite form than that, I think we shall have to continue to rely upon the opinions of our officers.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, my submission is that subsection 3-of course I realize that the hon. gentleman is merely inviting suggestions not for the purpose of giving them consideration, because I found that to be the case in the past-I suggest that subsection 3 in its present form and paragraphs (a) and (b) reduce themselves to a nullity by reason of the particularity and detail given. It is not for me to draft the exact words, but I submit this: that no dealer shall refuse to sell or supply an article or commodity to any person without justification. That will place the dealer in a position so that the crown will not have to establish all of the details, but the onus will still remain on it. It will not have to establish all of the details set forth in paragraphs (a) and (b).
Booking at this, I must say I would be very interested in the first prosecution under this section, provided a company or a dealer did not keep records indicating that the reason for the denial of a sale was that an intended purchaser had refused to resell or to offer to resell at a price not less than a minimum specified by the dealer or established by agreement. If all a dealer does is notify an intended purchaser that on and after a certain date he is on a quota; if he says "We feel that we have sufficient sales elsewhere, and do not have to deal with you. We appreciate the value of your patronage and respectfully decline it", I say there is no court in the country that would convict a dealer in the face of those circumstances. That would be

Combines Investigation Act the condition unless, as suggested by the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine, the dealer were foolish enough to give reasons either in the letter he might write, or in a memorandum, or in a conversation between his agents and the intended purchaser.
This has all the earmarks of being ineffective. With the greatest respect to those to whom the hon. member has made reference I say that, on the face of it, as the section now stands it will be ineffectual and inoperative; because these people of whom the Minister of Justice speaks with such awe, corporations with powerful counsel, are not going to have their records cluttered up with admissions of guilt or anything in the nature of statements that would come within the provisions of the section in question.
The situation is different under the Combines Investigation Act as a whole. The hon. member for Charlotte mentioned that a combination is sufficient. But the Minister of Justice quickly clarified that suggestion by stating that a combination, in itself, is no offence. Any number of manufacturers or distributors can combine or join together for the purpose of merchandising, so long as they have not the intent, or so long as their actions are not detrimental to the consumer. That was not very difficult to prove-although the Minister of Justice has said that it was-as compared with proving or establishing an offence under this new section. There is a vast gulf in between. One is comparatively easy. But I have read and reread the section, and I suggest that the difficulty the crown will have in discharging its onus by bringing a case within the provisions of subsections 3 (a) and (b), in their present form, is insurmountable so far as the prosecution is concerned. That would be so except in the isolated case where the smaller fellow, without legal talent available to him, may not cover himself. But any group of individuals desiring to evade this amendment and avoid its consequences, in so far as goods for future delivery are concerned, I submit will have very little to fear.
Having said that, I leave it to the minister to either make it effectual or leave it in its present form, as I know he will. But I am confident that when the first prosecution occurs some of my criticism will be justified by what takes place in the court; because it is obvious on the face of it that under the section as drafted the crown has piled upon itself an onus the discharge of which is almost impossible.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I suggest the difficulty of
proof will not be as great as has been suggested, because one will be able to proceed by a process of elimination. We will suppose that manufacturer A has been supplying retailer B over a certain period of years, and that suddenly he refuses to supply the retailer any longer. Retailer B is your witness, and counsel will ask him: "Have you been paying regularly? Have you behaved as a retailer should behave toward his supplier?" It will be relatively easy, by a process of elimination, to establish that the only reason the manufacturer has refused to supply goods is the one foreseen by this measure.
One should not forget that in a prosecution of this kind the retailer can be called as a witness. One does not have to rely upon the evidence from the manufacturer. The hon. member for Lake Centre has referred to the difficulty of getting evidence from the manufacturer's records, but I suggest to him that a prosecutor would not have to rely upon that; because in a case like that, if you are going to prosecute it will be because the manufacturer has refused to supply the retailer. The retailer will not be very happy about it and will gladly cooperate with the department. I do not see any great difficulty in the section.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: The minister has been referring to the matter of enforcement. How would it apply to dealers who in fact purchase and pay for goods they are to resell, although they are called commission agents? I understand that the enforcement of this measure with respect to a retailer depends largely upon whether he is in fact an independent retailer or dealer, or whether he is an agent in the true sense of the term. What about the man who takes a commission agency, but in fact has to pay for the goods as he receives them, or on a monthly basis? How will the measure apply? He has paid for the goods, although he is described as the agent of the manufacturer.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I may have used the wrong expression. I think I used the word "commission", but I meant to say that it would be on consignment.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: If the goods are on consignment, then I believe the title would remain in the manufacturer until the sale had actually taken place. And it might be that under an arrangement of that sort the conditions to be imposed would not contravene the act. But if my hon. friend will recall the answer I gave previously he will know they all related to a case where there was a transfer of title from the manufacturer to the dealer, who became the owner of the goods. When he became the owner of the goods he had the right to say what the selling price of the goods belonging to him would be. If the title remains in the manufacturer until the time it passes to the consumer, I think in that case the manufacturer would have the right to name his own selling price.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Would that cover service station operators and motorcar dealers?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: My understanding, and I may be wrong about it, is that a great many filling stations are owned and operated by the oil companies, by employees under the direction of the oil companies.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: There may be some, but I am thinking of the genuine dealer who owns his own establishment, who sells a certain brand of motor oil and gas at prices fixed by the oil company. It is his business; it is his property; he owns it, but with respect to the gas and oil he sells at prices fixed by the supplier.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will agree that even in those cases where the oil company is not operating the filling station but where they have a lessee who gets a quantity of oil and gas from the oil company, title to which remains in the oil company until it is sold-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: He pays for it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: It depends upon whether the manufacturer is selling his own goods direct to the purchaser or whether there is the intervention of another dealer who becomes the owner of those goods.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I should like to deal with the specific basis on which these dealers operate. They own their own business and are supplied by an oil company with a certain line of oil and gas which they have to sell at a certain price. They are not acting as agents of the oil company. They pay for their supplies as
Combines Investigation Act they are received, or in some cases on a weekly basis, or in exceptional cases I believe on a monthly basis. They do not act as agents because they have to pay for their supplies. Although they are described in some cases as being agents of the oil company, would such persons be subject to the provisions of this bill?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: If the dealer purchases the goods outright and then sells them he would come under the amendment, but not so if title to the goods remained in the manufacturer up to the time of the sale to the purchaser.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I think there is one aspect of this discussion that perhaps has not been sufficiently emphasized. The government is putting this measure forward with great determination. It is the obligation of the government, first, to know what the effect of this legislation is going to be and, second, to pass on to the members of this house information which the government possesses so the decision may be made with all the essential knowledge in the possession of the government.
It is the duty of members of this house to inform themselves adequately as to the effect of an amendment of this kind. I submit that the question which has been raised goes directly to the root of the problem we have before us. I ask the minister to tell us what is the exact situation in regard to the handling of oil and gasoline. After all, before bringing this bill forward he must have examined each of the great broad groups of merchandising and found out how they operated. I know he would not introduce this bill without having thoroughly considered every aspect. I think he should tell us now just how oil and gasoline is handled and what the impact of this amendment will be. We will then pass on to some other type of merchandise.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I do not think the most omniscient of governments could be expected to know all the operations and all the arrangements which oil companies may have with their dealers. I think most hon. members out of their common knowledge will bear me out when I say there are a number of cases in which oil companies operate filling stations with their own paid employees who are under their direction. The title of the goods remains with the manufacturer until they are sold direct to the motorist. That group would not fall within the terms of the amendment.
There is another larger group where the oil company has an arrangement with lessees of filling stations owned by it, under which the lessees are required to maintain the
2474	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act premises. The oil company agrees to supply the lessee from time to time with oil and gasoline as required, which he in turn sells to his customers. Regardless of what name we may give to that transaction, if the lessee, the filling station operator, or whatever appellation you wish to apply to him buys the oil and gasoline from the oil company direct, pays for it and resells it to the motorist, that transaction would come within the present amendment.
I do not know that I can make it any clearer. I am willing to continue to try to meet the quite reasonable requests of the leader of the opposition, but I think that pretty well covers the field.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Will not the result of this amendment be to drive manufacturers and retailers into a principal and agent relationship, which would not be subject to the provisions of this bill? In order to preserve his competitive position as against his opponents, the powerful retail chains, departmental stores and so on, will independent retailers not tend somehow or other to give their transactions with their suppliers the colour of a principal and agent relationship rather than that of an independent retailer buying from a manufacturer? Surely that will be the effect of this legislation.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I do not pretend to answer that question with any particular competence because it has to do with the motor trade and I am not an expert in that field.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Any type of trade.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Let us talk about one trade at a time. My answer to my hon. friend's question, for what it may be worth, is no, I do not think so. My impression is that the retailing of oil and gasoline is a pretty competitive business. With conditions as they are at the present time it is rather unlikely that any filling station operator would attempt to reduce the price of his merchandise in order to keep going.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: The avenue is open.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: If there is competition in the field at all it would seem to me to more likely be by companies like the Joy Oil Company, which has introduced some element of competition at the manufacturing level.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
The minister has just said that this particular field is pretty competitive, with which I agree, although it is subject to resale price maintenance, as he has just said. In the case of the independent dealers I would say the majority buy their gas, pay for it and then resell it. The minister admits it is a pretty competitive business. However, he has said it is going to be subject


to the bill. I cannot see how he can reconcile his two statements and say that the object of the bill is to increase competition when he says on the other hand that this particular business, which is subject to resale price maintenance, is pretty highly competitive.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I do not think I said it was
subject to resale price maintenance.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
The minister did not say
that in so many words but in fact it is.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
It is all very well for the
hon. member to say that, but do not imply that I have said it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Is the minister saying that it
is not?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
No, I am not saying it is or
it is not because it has not been necessary for us to inform ourselves on that point.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I think the answer the minister has just given is simply further proof that every effort that has been made to obtain reconsideration of the bill has been more than amply justified. We are dealing now with the effect of a specific section of the bill. Previously we were dealing with the broad question of whether a bill in this form should be adopted. Now we are dealing with the specific section and its effect upon the retailing of merchandise and commodities of various kinds. They divide themselves into many fields, and we are dealing with one very important field. In view of the fact that we as members of the House of Commons are asked to support a measure which is going to define as a criminal offence agreements to carry forward certain practices that have been going on for some time, I feel sure the minister would not come before the house and ask us to adopt a bill in this form without having had an inquiry made into the impact upon every one of the major groups of retail sales in this country.
Certainly one of the important groups that would immediately present itself to anyone would be the merchandising of gasoline and oil. Therefore it is not for the minister to say: I do not pose as an expert;
I do not say it will have this effect and I do not say it will not have this effect. I think it is for the minister to say to us that certainly they have examined the impact of the bill in this form on the merchandising arrangements of the country. When he is asked what the effect is in regard to gasoline or oil he should be able to say: This is what we have found it will be. If he is asked what the effect will be with respect to another type of merchandising he should be

able to say: I will tell you that. It is in relation to this very important type of merchandising that these questions are being asked. Either the minister knows what the broad division of this type of merchandising is or he does not. If he does, then he should inform us. If he does not, then at this point he should admit he has not the information upon which he should proceed at this time.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Probably if the opposition
would take a case that was not hypothetical but practical the minister would be able to give a concrete answer. The position with respect to service stations is that if you own your service station generally one of the oil companies will offer to instal the equipment if you will sell their product. Once you have agreed to do so, then if you are in a position where they will accept your credit they will fill your gasoline storage tank and you may pay them by cheque. If your credit is not so good you will order so many gallons of gasoline, submit a cheque and when it is cashed they will then put the gasoline in the tank. As the minister has said, in a general way, if the service station owner buys and pays for the gasoline he can sell it for whatever price he wishes.
I think his answer was absolutely satisfactory to anyone who understands the trade. I should like to point out further to hon. members of the house who have witnessed gasoline price wars-and I think most hon. members have had some experience on this subject-that surely no one would think that when gas price wars have taken place the brunt has been borne by the lessee or owner of the service station. His profit is far too small, even if he worked for nothing, for him to take part in the gas wars that we have seen take place. They are carried on by the companies. I have never seen any price fixing in this trade. I think it is most unfair to ask the minister to build up an answer to a mythical case, to have an answer prepared for a case that does not exist.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I should
like to give a practical case. In the city of St. John's, where there are about 60,000 people, there is an agency for Studebaker, one for Ford, one for Chevrolet, one for Pontiac and so on for other cars. There are several hundred parts in a motorcar. What is to prevent a dealer charging a higher price in the future than he has been charging up to now under catalogue prices?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
He would be prevented by
the amendment which provides that the manufacturer, if he wishes, may fix a maximum price for his product and may enforce
Combines Investigation Act that maximum price. Therefore if a dealer in St. John's were trying to charge the public more than the present suggested price the manufacturer would only have to fix a maximum price and he could prevent that.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
But if he
does not fix it?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: If he does not fix it then he must concur in whatever happens.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I should like to follow up the motion we were discussing a few moments ago. I was dealing with the oil business, but let us leave that and turn to the electrical appliance manufacturing field. I understand from what the minister has said that if the retailer buys and pays for the goods himself and then resells them, that transaction, as between him and the manufacturer, would be subject to the bill now before us. If he is an agent of the manufacturer then the transaction between them would not be subject to the bill. To repeat my question, does the minister not believe that if these retailers and manufacturers are interested in preserving their competitive position as against more powerful business concerns the tendency will be for the retailer to take on the colour of an agent so he can continue to get the benefit of resale price maintenance which he feels is the protection he needs against unfair competitive practices of large concerns?

speechtext: Again my answer is no; and again, notwithstanding what the leader of the opposition has said, I cannot honestly claim for myself any great competence in the field of merchandising of electrical appliances. The reason I say no is that when the bill comes into effect I think there is going to be in the electrical appliance field, as indeed there is now in respect of importations from the United States, a competitive area. Therefore the manufacturer who wishes to set up these agency arrangements will have to face this other competition. He may now have a very fine price-maintenance agreement with his own people but with a substantial part of the whole area open to this competition he is going to have to face it and, as was seen during the depression when resale price maintenance was in effect, if conditions get tough enough resale price maintenance will not stand up under it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I should like to make the observation that resale price maintenance was certainly not in effect in the depression in the same way it is today. I should like to put before the minister the other alternative and ask whether he does not think

Combines Investigation Act the situation may develop that even if retailers do not willingly become agents of manufacturers, yet manufacturers will be forced into the retail field, which would have the same effect of lessening competition rather than increasing it?
In that connection I want to lay before him the evidence given on this very point in the committee by the witness from the Canadian Manufacturers Association, as reported at page 575 of the proceedings. He was being questioned by Mr. Fleming:
Q. My last point is in regard to your statement that the abolition of resale price maintenance will force manufacturers into the retail business. Can you be more specific about that so we can estimate the degree of danger or the extent to which that might become a practice on the part of manufacturers?
A. Mr. Fleming, you are asking me to deal with a situation we have never had to face. As I see it, we would have to adopt the merchandising tactics of, for instance, the Singer Sewing Machine Company, in that we would open our own stores in various places. If you decided to buy a McClary refrigerator you would go to one of those stores, owned and operated by us. We could not possibly provide as many stores as now sell McClary refrigerators but we would try to provide enough to give us a satisfactory volume of business.
Q. What would be the effect on prices, eventually, to the consumer?
A. Well, sir, unless we proved to be more efficient retailers than the retailers in business now, the price would not be any lower. I, myself, have had a long and assorted business experience and I am a little inclined to think that there are very few people who have a talent for manufacturing and who have a talent for retailing also.
Q. Well, in short-[DOT]
A. I am sure that we would not be any more efficient than the average good retailer today-and consequently we could not sell at any lower price.
The minister has been saying that if the relationship of the supplier and the dealer is maintained, then! the transaction will come under the effect of this bill and price maintenance will not be allowed to continue. What I am putting before the minister is that we have had evidence to the effect that the desire of the retailers for the protection of price maintenance is such that when they find that as dealers they are deprived of it as a result of this bill but can get it as agents, they will become agents of the manufacturers instead of dealers. Furthermore, if that process does not take place, then the manufacturers themselves will go into the retail business. There we have the evidence of a manufacturer who says he does not think they would be efficient retailers, but nevertheless they might have to undergo that process. If this bill is enforced, according to this witness it will not increase competition but will really substantially reduce it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES

The whole situation must be read in the light of the witness's earlier answer, which I read. His earlier answer was that, notwithstanding the difficulty, if resale price maintenance is abolished he thinks there is danger that manufacturers may be forced into the retail business. The minister

appears to have overlooked that answer, so I shall read it again. He read only those parts of the answer which supported his own argument, but the whole answer does not support his argument for the very good reason that the whole answer was subject to the earlier question and answer.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member this question. If the manufacturer says he cannot see any profit in retailing, why would he worry about getting into the retail business at all as long as he gets his manufacturer's selling price? That is his business. Why should he worry about retailing at all?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Because the point that was being made in the committee was that if resale price maintenance is abolished there is danger that many retailers will find they are not able to stay in business. They will be driven to the wall by the large concerns, and will not be able to take the manufacturer's goods at all. The manufacturer, in self-protection, will be forced into the retail business. This point was made over and over again in the committee, and I am sorry it did not register with the minister. The manufacturers, to protect themselves against the big department stores who want to be the sole outlets for these lines, would have to set up their own retail stores because they do not want-any more than the small merchant wants-to be at the mercy of the big giants in the retail field. They want the little retailer kept in the field. It is in the interests of the consuming public also to see the little retailer kept in business.
The point made by this witness is that if resale price maintenance is abolished the protection the little merchant has will be abolished and he will be driven to the wall, and the manufacturer will be in the position of finding retail outlets only through these giant stores. In self-protection the manufacturers will then be driven to setting up their own retail outlets. It was in the light of the earlier answer of the witness that he felt they may be forced to do that, that he made his later answer. And he was then asked: Supposing you did have to go into the retail field and set up your retail stores, what would be the effect on price? The witness said: We are not as efficient at retailing as the retailers now in the business, so the price would not come down.
The important part of this witness's evidence, which the minister overlooked, was to the effect that if resale price maintenance is removed the manufacturers may be driven into providing their own retail outlets rather than get into the hands of these giants who would now dominate the field.

I should like to say a word. The hon. member for Lake Centre made a suggestion which I think is worthy of consideration. He pointed to the fact that the clauses as now drafted are restrictive in their nature and that nothing in the present bill would entitle a retailer, whether it be a co-operative society or an individual, to get supplies from a manufacturer. He suggested that there should be a subclause to the effect that no dealer shall refuse to sell or supply an article or commodity without justification. It seems that would cover the whole field. I think it strengthens the suggestion we have tried to put before the house all during this debate, namely that there should be some public board to which the retailer, the manufacturer or the consumer could apply if he felt that he was not getting the kind of deal he should get from a manufacturer. If there is difficulty about the phrase "without justification", as there might be, the board, having considered the application and whether or not there was justification, would make a decision and that decision might be appealed to a court of law. In that way we would be getting nearer what would be just to all those interested in measures of this kind.
What I am afraid of-and the more I hear of the discussion the more fear I have-is that as the section is now drafted it is not sufficiently comprehensive, and that it does not do what many of us would like to see done under this kind of legislation, namely give everyone as just a deal as possible and enable retailers, co-operative societies and so on to get goods they could resell without having to maintain the price laid down by the manufacturer. The evil we are trying to cure, and I know it is an evil, is that there is price control on the part of private individuals, namely manufacturers. That idea is abhorrent to all of us. On the other hand I think we must be careful that we give to all those interested in merchandising-the consumer, the manufacturer and the retailer- the opportunity of competing for the business that exists, and give the consumer a squarer deal than he is getting at the present time.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES

I suggest, however, in all seriousness that if we are going to have any

Combines Investigation Act regard for civil liberties, about which the hon. member for Lake Centre is always so solicitous, of the individual citizen, then in creating a new crime we must set some kind of a definition or some kind of criterion of improper conduct. If we merely say, as he suggested, that no dealer shall refuse to sell or supply an article or commodity to any other person without justification, period, what kind of a prosecution would that be, if I may ask? You lay the charge and it comes before the judge and you say: "Well, he did this without justification". "All right", the court will say, "what is justification? What is proper justification?" Surely the hcxn. member for Lake Centre was not serious when he made that suggestion in the first place. If he says this bill is in bad shape as it is now worded, I would say it would be much worse if this suggestion of his were accepted, because there would be no kind of adequate standard in the creation of a new crime if you merely added the words "without justification". What would justification be? Could any person tell us? There would be no kind of objective act, thought or thing in relation to which justification, as defined as such in the section, could be applied. When we are amending the Combines Investigation Act for the purpose of abolishing resale price maintenance, if we are going to be halfway fair to the subject at all and are going to protect his civil liberties, what we must do is define in definite terms the crime we are committing or rather creating and with which we are proposing to charge him before the law.
