maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
My hon. friend says it would be difficult to enforce this legislation. I wonder if he has looked at subsection 2 of section 37A, which reads as follows:
No dealer shall directly or indirectly by agreement, threat, promise or any other means whatsoever, require or induce or attempt to require or induce any other person to resell an article or commodity . . .


I will not list the other provisions. If the dealer does so, it will be in breach of the act. That means that when this implement firm goes out in the spring to make arrangements with its dealers, it cannot enter into an arrangement directly or indirectly, or by any other means whatever, under which there is any implication or understanding that a resale price is to be maintained on its products. That is what it says to start with. If they do that, a charge can be laid under that section.
Suppose the gentleman who is their dealer has obtained a list of the goods on which they have suggested what the resale price shall be, and suppose he sells them for less than the suggested* mark-up. This would not take place in a vacuum by itself-from a common sense point of view what would most likely happen is this. If the dealer was a reasonably good man and did it once, they would probably have their block man go around and have a little chat with him about prices. If he did it again they might have another chat. They would not immediately chop off the man who had been a good dealer for them for many years. The time would come, however, when if this little friendly coercion, that had been applied did not produce any acceptable response, then they would refuse to supply him with any more goods. Then the dealer would come in to the combines investigation branch and make a complaint and we would investigate it.
My hon. friend says there would be great difficulty as compared with the administration of the Combines Investigation Act. In the case of the Combines Investigation Act we have to go out and get 100 per cent of our evidence from witnesses who are unwilling, from beginning to end, to have anything to do with our investigation. In the case of a prosecution under this amendment the retailer himself is a willing and able witness to assist the crown. He will say that on such and such a date the block man or the salesman spoke to him, and that he spoke with him at another time and then, two or three weeks afterward, his supplies were refused. He will say: It is true they have not said that they have refused supplies for that reason, but I have every reason to believe that is the case.
Notwithstanding what has been said by my hon. friend, who is a lawyer with great experience in criminal law, this is a pure question of fact, as I think he will admit. Under those circumstances if we put the dealer into the witness box, proved what had happened and subpoenaed the block man or the salesman, if the accused corporation was

unable to give any other reasonable explanation as to why suddenly, after some lengthy period of experience, they had refused to give any further supplies, I should think there would not be too much difficulty in getting the judge to hold, under the circumstances, that an offence had been proved under this act. In any event I am perfectly certain that the suggestion which my hon. friend from Lake Centre has made is no improvement.

speechtext: It is quite obvious from the answers we have received that the talk we have heard from the government about this bill being designed to stimulate competition is just so much idle nonsense, because it is perfectly apparent from what the minister himself has just admitted that the net effect of this bill is going to be to build up more monopolies and reduce effective competition. It is crystal clear now; the minister has just indicated it by his last remarks, and it is perfectly apparent what course business is likely to take in this country. speechtext:
I should like to turn to another aspect of the proposed section 37A. It is an aspect which seems to me to be of very great importance because it contemplates a complete departure from the principle of the

Combines Investigation Act. One would have thought that, as this measure is put forward as an amendment of the Combines Investigation Act, it would be designed to be in keeping with the principle of the act, but it is not in this very important respect.
Section 2 of the Combines Investigation Act is the one which contains important definitions. It defines a combine as a combination having certain described attributes or a merger, trust or monopoly. Then follow these very important words:
. . . which combination, merger, trust or monopoly, has operated or is likely to operate to the detriment or against the interest of the public, whether consumers, producers or others.
It is inherent in every provision of the Combines Investigation Act illegalizing combinations, mergers, trusts or monopolies that the prohibition or illegalization is not absolute. It is only partial or conditional. In other words, before any combination, merger, trust or monopoly is one within the meaning of the Combines Act it is necessary for the prosecution to establish that such combination, merger, trust or monopoly has operated or is likely to operate to the detriment or against the interests of the public, whether consumer, producer or others. That provision has been in the act ever since it was first enacted, and so far as I know that principle has never been questioned in this house.
If one is to look at Bill No. 36 in that light, one finds in if a complete departure from that principle. There is nothing in the proposed section 37A which imports that qualification into this provision. The proposed section 37A does not deal with combinations, mergers, trust or monopolies as defined in section 2 of the Combines Investigation Act. This proposed section takes up a new subject, and deals with it in terms of absolute prohibition. I submit to you, sir, that departure from the principle of the act is not sound.
I call to mind some of the evidence tendered before the committee on that very subject. When the representatives of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada appeared before the committee-and may I say that theirs was one of the best and most intelligent presentations with which the committee was favoured-Mr. Bengough, the president, and Mr. Wismer, the director of public relations and research of that estimable organization, had something to say on this subject. I refer now to page 372 of -the proceedings of the committee where I asked some questions dealing with this particular matter:
Q. May I ask Mr. Wismer if he feels that this so-called practice of price maintenance is a detriment to or perhaps in harmony with public interest?
Combines Investigation Act
A. I think we can say this, in so far as the deal is made privately and enforced privately we would have to say no, but where it is a general practice I think we would have to have a lot more information.
Q. Have you examined the draft bill on page 34 of the proceedings of this committee?
A. I have read the original draft.
May I interject to say that the original draft was, to all intents and purposes, in the same form as Bill No. 36. There was no difference whatever in form, so far as the point I am discussing is concerned.
Q. You will recall it purports to propose blanket prohibition on resale prices. Would you think that is a proper and desirable way of going about this matter, that we have blanket prohibition, or if we are going to have legislation on it should it be left to determine whether in the particular case the particular type of agreement is in the given circumstances harmful to the public interest or not?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: It would have to be flexible.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
You wouldn't favour a general
prohibition?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
No.
Mr. Bengough was not the only witness who appeared before the committee who entertained that opinion. At the moment I am not dealing with the other shortcomings of this legislation or with the failure to provide concomitant legislation to deal with the vicious practices I discussed earlier, such as loss-leadering. We are dealing here with the neat question as to whether this amendment of the Combines Investigation Act should be written in terms of a blanket prohibition, without regard to any necessity whatever of proof that the practice is harmful or detrimental to the public interest. In that respect the bill, as I have said, is a complete departure from the principle of the 'Combines Investigation Act.
It is no answer to say that in the course of judicial interpretation, if the combine has some of the attributes set forth in section 2, subsection 1 of the Combines Investigation Act, that will import, so far as the courts are concerned, that the combination is operating or is likely to operate to the detriment or against the interest of the public, whether consumers, producers or others. I submit that is no answer to the point we are dealing with here, where we have a section which is imported into the act, a section which does not deal with combinations, mergers, trusts or monopolies, but deals with a particular practice which we are told obtains today in certain lines of merchandising.
I submit that if there is anything to be said for legislation of this kind-I am not yielding anything of what I said about this bill-then certainly it can only be contemplated by the house on the basis that it should be within the principle of the main act. What objection could there be to carry-

Combines Investigation Act ing into this proposed section 37A the principle of the Combines Investigation Act that measures dealt with under the act or frowned upon under the act are made illegal only where it is proven affirmatively by the crown that they operate or are likely to operate to the detriment or against the interests of the public? Surely this legislation could not be supported seriously by the government on any basis other than that the government was prepared to assume on behalf of the crown, in any prosecution under the proposed section 37A, the burden and duty of establishing that in that particular case the practice frowned upon was operating to the detriment of the public. I submit, therefore, there are no reasons against preserving the integrity of this essential principle of the Combines Investigation Act. There is no reason for departing from it. I contend that if this legislation is to be entertained by the house, it must be made subject to that essential principle of the act, and its present terms of blanket prohibition must be revised accordingly.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the short answer to the point my hon. friend has raised is that the Combines Investigation Act forbids combinations that are undue and against the interests of the public. What my hon. friend has overlooked, I suggest with deference, is that the courts have consistently declared that any substantial lessening of competition is undue and against the interests of the public. In the case of vertical resale price maintenance, the Mac-Quarrie committee came to the conclusion, and so recommended to the government, that having regard to the present growth of the practice, it does substantially eliminate competition and is therefore contrary to the public interest. On that account it is unnecessary to include this ingredient in the prohibition of resale price maintenance.

That contention has not had the effect of wiping out these words in the act. These words are still part of the act. Nobody has proposed that these words should be eliminated from the act; yet the government now


proposes that an amendment be made to the act which will not be subject to these restrictive words.
The minister is not prepared, I gather, to have this amendment made subject to those words which qualify all the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act in relation to combinations, mergers, trusts and monopolies. If the minister is so confident that the practice is detrimental to the public interest, do you not think he would be quite prepared to submit to the burden of proving that fact to the court and having the court make a finding to that effect?

In effect he would be saying, "Go to it, boys, and make your own deal with each one of these dealers." In ordinary terms of he trade, that seems to me an unrealistic approach to the thing. It seems to me that if you are advertising a motorcar or any major piece of equipment needed for the house, you are advertising it at a price. You would seem to be saying this is the quality of the goods and this is the maximum price, but get it for what you can. Combines Investigation Act In point of fact it is going to be very confusing, and very difficult to establish a proper price to pay for a stove or something like that of a certain quality.

If you have a suggested price and a maximum price, it seems to me you are going to have quite a bit of confusion in the merchandising of this type of equipment. Whether it is good or bad economics, or whether it is good or bad socially or any other way, it seems to me you are going to have a certain amount of confusion which is not desirable.

In that regard I would like particularly to refer to the evidence of Mr. Bengough, president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, when he was being questioned by the committee. He was asked
Combines Investigation Act what, in his view, should be done about this practice. At page 372 of the proceedings we find this question:
What is your view; would you agree that it would only be fair, if we are going to introduce legislation to outlaw in blanket fashion all price maintenance agreements, that we should at the same time introduce legislation to prevent the loss-leader practice?
To that Mr. Bengough replied:
"I think it would be vital it should be done."
What we are concerned about here is that we are confronted with legislation which, without any necessity on the part of the crown to prove that a particular price maintenance agreement operates to the detriment of the public, makes the general practice of resale price maintenance illegal. If that becomes law, there will be no method left by which an individual retailer, or retailers in general, can protect themselves against the practice of loss leaders. I do not think any member opposite cani deny that statement. If this practice of resale price maintenance is outlawed, as it will be by this legislation, there is no method by which the retailer as an individual or retailers as a class can protect themselves against the loss-leader practice. Therefore the question surely is pertinent: by what alternative method does the government intend to protect retailers against the loss-leader practice? Because it has been proven to be the greatest threat against the existence of the individual independent retailer.
I am not going to read again the evidence I placed upon record before with regard to the findings of the royal commission on price spreads. Mr. Chairman, the matter that has been raised by my hon. friend is one that exercises the minds of retail merchants everywhere in this country. I would point out particularly that it is a matter of concern to the retail merchants of Saskatchewan and their organization in that province. One of the requests they have made-it is a reasonable one, and should not be treated in the cavalier and disrespectful manner shown by some hon. members-should be faced squarely and fairly. The retail merchants of Saskatchewan were denied the opportunity of presenting their arguments in support of their brief. One of the things they fear particularly is set forth in the current issue of the Western Retailer. I refer to the question of loss leaders, which has been discussed by the hon. member for Kamloops.
This brief, prepared by Mr. R. E. Walker, a man of long experience in the retail trade before he became chairman of the retail merchants association of Saskatchewan, requests information from the government as to what would be done to protect the retail merchants from the dangerous possibility of loss leaders. The Minister of Justice has said that his experience and that of the government is that there is nothing to fear at this time, with economic conditions as they are today. In the brief of the retail merchants of Saskatchewan the following appears:
We have long maintained that we can compete-
And when they say "we" they mean the independents.
-with mass merchandisers if they will refrain or preferably if they are prevented from instituting unfair practices which are not within our capacity to meet.
And the unfair practice to which reference is made at the present time is the practice of loss leaders.
We submit, gentlemen, that resale price maintenance has had the effect of restraining mass buyers from such unfair practices and which has done so, as we have attempted to demonstrate, at no cost to the public, as confirmed by the royal commission on prices of 1949. And we further submit that if resale price maintenance is declared illegal,-
By "illegal" apparently is meant if it is set aside by parliament.
-that there can be no effective legislation, confirmed by the Stevens report, to curb these vicious unfair practices so clearly demonstrated and recognized by this commission. We think it would be of interest to this committee to discover whether the Hon. Lester B. Pearson and the Hon. James L. Ilsley, both of whom have served as cabinet ministers in the present government, and both of whom were members of the royal commission on price spreads-	*


The hon. gentleman was secretary of that commission, as I remember.
*-would testify that the conclusions which they arrived at through a study of the history of many, many years of business, were only valid for a temporary period, or whether they consider these conclusions to remain valid.
The conclusions to which reference is made were those reached by the Stevens commission, and they were as follows:
The competitors of the store using the loss leaders are, however, the persons chiefly affected. That the deliberate use of cut prices to draw patronage away from competitors is an unfair trade practice, is quite clear. Such reductions are not prompted by any desire to serve the public by giving lower prices. One purpose is to attract customers to whom the store hopes to sell goods that are not loss leaders, at substantial profits. Another purpose is to create the illusion of lower prices on all articles. That this end is not always attained does not in any way lessen the unfairness of good practice.

speechtext: I cannot imagine any set of circumstances under which a group of farmers or an individual farmer has ever attempted to impose resale price maintenance upon his products. I should be glad if my hon. friend could give us a concrete example of that sort of thing.

speechtext:

board would be a concrete example.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I thought perhaps that was what my hon. friend was referring to. The hon. member for Annapolis-Kings asked that question earlier today.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I know he did.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: My answer was that if the marketing board was set up under provincial legislation, it would not be affected by this proposed legislation.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
That opinion is extremely interesting. What is the foundation for it? Is it just an offhand opinion by the minister, or is that an opinion from the law officers? There is certainly nothing whatsoever in any portion of the Combines Investigation Act that exempts any provincial marketing board. The minister, in an offhand way, has said they are not covered by this legislation because that is a matter of provincial legislation. As to the marketing boards in the provinces, they will come within the definition of dealer. No exception whatever is made in the act, and there is nothing whatever that will deny the application of this bill in its present form, as I see it, unless something is done to exempt provincial marketing boards. As a matter of fact an exemption is made under section 498A of the Criminal Code to cover certain co-operatives because of this very difficulty. Section 498A, subsection (a) indicates as follows:
The provisions of this paragraph shall not, however, prevent a co-operative society returning to producers or consumers, or a co-operative wholesale society returning to its constituent retail members, the whole or any part of the net surplus made in its trading operations in proportion to purchases made from or sales to the society . . .
Those co-operative organizations can be set up under provincial law just as marketing boards are today set up under provincial

law. I believe my hon. friend has raised a point that is worthy of serious consideration, namely the degree to which this amendment in its present haphazard form may result in provincial marketing boards finding themselves in jeopardy. I think the minister should welcome the suggestion of an amendment in that connection, to make that point positively clear. Certainly the fact that the provincial authorities set up a municipal board does not place that municipal board above any federal law. I think the hon. member for Queens has raised a point and has directed the attention of the minister to a question that deserves more serious consideration than will have been given by an offhand opinion, unless that offhand opinion is based on the law officers of the crown having definitely indicated that, in their opinion, the section as amended will not apply to any marketing board.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Before the minister answers, I should like to ask my hon. and genial friend, the hon. member for Lake Centre, if he will agree that the function of the Minister of Justice is equivalent, mutatis mutandis, to that of the Lord Chancellor in England.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: What has England to do with this matter? We run our own parliament.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: My hon. friend does not understand who the Lord Chancellor of England is. I am just arguing a most important point with the hon. member for Lake Centre. Ke will agree that the Minister of Justice occupies a similar position and performs a function similar to that performed by the Lord Chancellor in England.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I agree that he exercises some of the jurisdiction; but the Lord Chancellor is the head of the judicial system in Great Britain, and I am certainly glad that the Minister of Justice in this country is not in that position.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: I am satisfied that my hon. friend agrees with me partly, if not in to to; and I will tell him this. One day I spoke to Lord Hailsham who was then Lord Chancellor of England. I said to him: My lord, are you the guardian of the king? He said: No, I am the-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES

Combines Investigation Act

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: That is exactly what some of us had hoped. That is the reason we have been directing questions, in the expectation that finally we might get some evidence that he knows something about this bill.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice has given strong reasons why the argument that has been presented for some days, that this bill should not be dealt with in haste, should have been recognized by the government. He has indicated that there is a rather strange attitude toward the measures already on the statute books, including the only measure that can possibly deal with a threat of loss leaders which is relevant to the bill now before us. But I want to refer back to something the minister said this afternoon, because it requires some explanation. The hon. member for Lake Centre pointed out that in this case, uncertain though the terms may be, the bill now before us creates an absolute offence without any qualifications as to the motive or intent of the person who carried out the act that might be regarded as an offence against this measure. He suggested there should be some words as "without justification", or something of that kind, to indicate that the offence would only exist if in fact there was the spirit of mens rea in what had been done.

Combines Investigation Act The Minister of Justice said it was not possible or practical to introduce any such qualification, although the hon. member for Lake Centre had made it quite clear that he was not suggesting the exact words which should be used but rather that there should be some qualification which related to the wrong intent.
The explanation which has been given by the minister simply does not hold water, because there is the qualification that combinations, mergers, trusts or monopolies mentioned in section 2 of the Combines Investigation Act must be shown to have operated or to be likely to operate to the detriment or against the interest of the public, whether consumers, producers or others. The answer given by the minister is simply inconsistent with the operation of the act itself to which this is a proposed amendment. Then in the section of the Criminal Code mentioned before, section 498A, which deals with conspiracies in restraint of trade we find the words "unduly prevent or lessen competition". If in relation to transactions of this kind in other legislation the word "unduly" can be defined; if conduct that is likely to be detrimental to the public interest can be defined, then surely similar exceptions could be made in this legislation. Then it would be possible to deal with this with the likelihood that those who are carrying out some arrangement which in no way injures the public will not suffer because of the overriding prohibition contained in this legislation.
I suggest that the minister, even at this stage in the discussion, should reconsider his statement in that connection. It does not do his position justice that he should give an explanation which, if it is sound, means that we should have before us now amendments to the Combines Investigation Act removing those qualifications in regard to other combines, other joint enterprises, which certainly would be just as injurious in their effect.
The minister this afternoon gave one extremely interesting explanation of the nature of the grounds that might be employed by a dealer to deny to a retailer the things that he sought to buy and sell. One of the grounds was if the dealer maintained a slovenly establishment. This is the explanation given by the minister piloting the bill. speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
If that is the kind of ground
on which the protection that is supposed to be afforded to the dealer under this legislation can be avoided, then this legislation is certainly a fraud on the retailer as well as on the public.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if I have left
the impression which the leader of the opposition has just stated I would feel with him that the bill was an improper one. But I think he has misunderstood my remarks. At the present time the manufacturer may discontinue the arrangement he has with his dealers for a number of reasons. Amongst others, if he is manufacturing goods which have to be exposed for sale to advantage in a neat establishment, he may not want to continue selling to the retailer when he maintains a slovenly one. He may want to discontinue his arrangement with the retailer if the man becomes a poor credit risk and will not meet the manufacturer's bills, or he may have a variety of reasons. The present bill does not touch any of the existing reasons the manufacturer may have for discontinuing his arrangements with the retailer. The point I was making in the context of the remark my hon. friend has just quoted was that the only basis on which the manufacturer could be held to account under the proposed amendment is if he discontinues supplying the retailer with renewal goods because of the fact that the retailer has failed to maintain a price which the manufacturer has set. It is the same point that was raised just a few moments ago by the hon. member for York West; that is, if the manufacturer has some genuine reason outside the terms of the bill for wanting to discontinue his relationship with the retailer he is just as free to do so after the bill has been passed as he was before.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Some point does come where
it is perfectly obvious that any further attempt to tie the minister down to an explanation of this measure which will be in any way understandable simply has to be abandoned. I am satisfied the record will demonstrate that hon. members are

being called upon to adopt a measure which the minister has very clearly shown he does not understand himself, which he has shown beyond all doubt is most uncertain in its application, and which in fact he even tries to leave the impression may have very little effect at all. On the other hand, of course it will always be there as a warning to those he might find occasion to deal with.
To hear the minister at one point one would think this is a stern measure. To hear him at another point one would think this has no teeth in it at all. Recognizing the fact that every answer the minister has given has further confused the issue and demonstrated why this measure should not go through, I can only close by quoting these words from "Alice in Wonderland":
"When I use a word," Humpty Dumpty said, in rather a scornful tone, "it means just what I choose it to mean-neither more nor less."
You can almost hear the minister listening to questions across the floor, because in this case Humpty Dumpty was being questioned. I continue with the quotation:
"The question is," said Alice, "whether you can make words mean so many different things."
"The question is," said Humpty Dumpty, "which is to be master,-that's all."
And that is all that is in issue here. We heard before the statement: "If we want to get away with it, who is going to stop us?" At every stage the only real argument we have had is: If we want to get away with it, who is going to stop us? We recognize that we must bow to the weight of this majority.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think there are any farmers' co-operative organizations that set up resale prices. I do not think that there is any way in which co-operative organizations, as at present set up, can be affected by this particular legislation. You have already had that opinion from the minister. I do not think there is any reason whatsoever for delaying the legislation further.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated before, it is obvious that there is no advantage in further debate on this measure and I propose to move that this bill be not now read a third time. I do with the utmost earnestness urge members of this house, and particularly members on the other side, to recognize that during the whole of this committee discussion the evidence has mounted that the government has not yet adequately considered this measure.
The explanations given by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) are most conflicting misinterpretations of the real effect of this bill. I hope hon. members will look over the record and see the number of occasions the minister has directly contradicted himself as to the effect and application of this measure. I do not intend to pursue this. I only repeat that at one time the minister has sought to convey the impression that the bill would harm no one, and at another time that it was a stern measure designed to deal with people who were injuring the Canadian consumer.
It has been double-talk from the time we went into committee, as it was double-talk prior to that time. There has been no explanation given by the minister as to why this measure would not apply to agricultural organizations which are marketing products on a large scale. There has been no attempt by the minister to explain why marketing organizations right across the country engaged in every stage of marketing and establishing prices which they believe will be to the advantage of the producer will not come under the blanket prohibitions of this bill. There has been no evidence whatever why simple safeguards for the person who is harming no one should not be included. No reason has been given why there should not be an exception in the bill to provide that its provisions will apply only where what is done is contrary to the public interest or has unduly raised prices, as is included in the Combines Investigation Act and in the section of the Criminal Code which deals with a similar subject.

Combines Investigation Act
With all these facts before us; with all the evidence that has accumulated that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), who presents this bill, is not able to indicate to us that it contains safeguards or in fact will be effective for the purpose for which it has been said it was designed, I am moving an amendment as no mere delaying device but as a means of placing before the house the suggestion that the dignity of parliament be preserved by refusing to pass this measure into the law of the land now with so little evidence before us as to what its real effect will be. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton):
That Bill No. 36 be not now read a third time, but that it be read a third time this day six months hence.
